title: Public Service Decline and Support for the Populist Right: Evidence from England’s National Health Service
authors: ZACHARY P. DICKSON, SARA B. HOBOLT, CATHERINE DE VRIES, SIMONE CREMASCHI
abstract: The rise of populist right parties is well studied, but relatively little attention has been given to how public service performance influences voter support. Given that public services are often the primary means through which citizens interact with the state, we argue that declining public services can create grievances that increase the appeal of populist right parties. Focusing on England’s National Health Service, we combine administrative data on local health facility closures with panel data on public preferences and voting intentions. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that closures reduce satisfaction with public services and increase support for populist right parties. These effects are moderated by migrant registrations at local health practices, highlighting the interaction between public service performance and immigration concerns in fueling populist right support. Our findings underscore the role of public service decline as a driver of support for populist parties, especially in areas undergoing demographic change.

title: Divergent Legacies: How the Local Instantiation of National Conflict Conditions Postwar Political Engagement
abstract: Under what conditions does violence generate legacies of political [dis]engagement? Victimization is frequently linked to higher rates of political engagement – voting, protesting, attending meetings, etc. Often, however, victims withdraw from politics. These initial responses are evident generations later. I reconcile these disparate trends by analyzing the materialization of national conflict at the local level. When a community experiences violence perpetrated by non-local factions, victimization is more likely to politicize. By contrast, when perpetrated by members of one’s community against other local members, violence is more likely to depoliticize. To test these arguments, I leverage an original survey, archival material, and interviews from the understudied case of Cameroon. From 1956 to 1971, the Union des Populations du Cameroun (UPC) fought against French and Cameroonian state and paramilitary forces. Civilians were heavily targeted by the state, militias, and UPC guerillas. Today, variation in those local experiences is associated with differences in political behavior and socialization practices.

title: Two-Faced Janus: Party System Closure and Democracy in Asia
authors: Don S. Lee, Fernando Casal Bértoa
abstract: This article examines the impact of party system institutionalization (PSI) on the survival and quality of democracy in Asia. To the best of our knowledge, no research has ever tested these relationships using sophisticated statistical methods. To address this gap, this article analyzes an original dataset of PSI in twenty-four democratic party systems in Asia since the end of WWII, combined with the V-Dem dataset for a number of variables measuring the quality of democracy, such as liberal democracy and accountability. We find that PSI has a nuanced, curvilinear relationship with both survival and quality of democracy. As in the “Goldilocks” story, excessive systemic institutionalization can be as detrimental to democracy, both for its survival and quality, as party system inchoateness.

title: Immigration and the Slope of the Labour Demand Curve: The Role of Firm Heterogeneity in a Model of Regional Labour Markets
authors: Andrea Ariu, Tobias Müuller, Tuan Nguyen
abstract: In this paper, we provide new explanations for the puzzling findings that migrants do not decrease natives’ wages and that skilled immigration can increase them. We develop a model with regional labour markets and heterogeneous firms in which workers of different skill levels are imperfect substitutes, but for a given skill level, natives and migrants are perfect substitutes within a firm. In this setting, a skilled labour supply shock due to immigration induces skill-intensive firms to expand. These across-firm reallocations reduce the within-firm substitution between skilled and unskilled workers, thus limiting relative wage adjustments. When this mechanism is coupled with human capital externalities that are skill-neutral at the firm level but skill-biased on aggregate, the same skilled immigration shock can increase absolute and relative skilled wages. These two mechanisms are quantitatively important: the negative impact of immigration on natives’ wages is reduced by at least one-third when the across-firm reallocation mechanism is at work, and human-capital externalities can revert the sign of this relation.

title: Welcome Home? The Role of Stayees in Return Migration
abstract: While most research on return migration focuses on return migrants' experiences, this article highlights the perspectives of stayee family members. Based on in‐depth interviews with 32 Polish stayees, it examines how they prepare for returnees' arrival and how they re‐adapt to their renewed presence, thereby supporting their reintegration into the society of origin. The analysis distinguishes two stages of receiving returnees back: the welcome stage, which is primarily concerned with practical arrangements and emotional preparedness, and the reception stage, in which returnees are further accompanied and assisted—or not—after arrival. The reception stage reveals two analytically distinct but often overlapping dimensions of stayees' practices: domestic and family inclusion, and socio‐economic inclusion. These forms of engagement vary with the strength of relationships and stayees' family positions. The findings show that return migration is a relational process involving both returnees and stayees, shaped by different understandings of responsibility and support.

title: Voices of Change: Low‐Skilled Migrant Workers' Perspectives on Labour Law Reforms in Qatar
authors: Šemsia Jatić, Abdoulaye Diop, Fahmida Naheen, Engi El‐Maghraby, Haneen Al‐Qassass, Buthaina Al Khelaifi
abstract: In the years preceding the 2022 FIFA World Cup, Qatar introduced a series of labour reforms aimed at strengthening migrant workers' rights, including the abolition of exit permit requirements, the removal of the No Objection Certificate requirement for job changes and the introduction of a universal minimum wage. Drawing on semi‐structured interviews with 30 low‐skilled male migrant workers conducted in October 2023, this study examines how workers perceived and experienced these reforms in their everyday lives. The findings reveal a nuanced picture that resists binary assessments of success or failure. Many participants described meaningful improvements in job mobility, freedom of movement and living conditions, particularly those who had spent many years in Qatar and were able to compare conditions before and after the reforms. However, the translation of legal change into everyday experience was uneven. Workers continued to navigate their rights through informal information networks, relationships with employers and unequal social and financial resources that often predate migration itself. By centring migrant workers' own voices, this study contributes to a more grounded understanding of labour reform as a socially embedded process shaped by relationships, unequal resources and the everyday contexts through which rights obtain meaning.

title: Naiveté or Strategic Ambiguity? Examining Economic, Demographic and Security Narratives in India's Refugee Policy
abstract: The decadal transition in the Indian politico‐legal stance on refugees, from a human rights tilt to national security concerns, invites a close examination. India maintains a theoretical safe distance from the international legal framework on refugees by not acceding to the 1951 Refugee Convention, while on the ground, it extensively engages—politically and judicially—with refugee‐related domestic legal issues. In the absence of a dedicated legal framework, the refugees, categorised based on temporalities and spatialities, face a highly unpredictable executive and judicial discretion. The present work critically examines the validity of three purported claims that India frames as ‘obstacles’ in enacting refugee‐specific legislation, using a mixed method design—combining doctrinal analysis of Indian jurisprudence, Parliamentary questions, statutory law and Executive Policy Rules along with a review of demographic data and securitization aspects to draw some hints as real‐world inferences on the actual impact caused by refugees.

title: Relationality and Temporality of Return Migration: Overseas Chinese Students During the COVID ‐19 Pandemic
abstract: This study applies the perspectives of relationality and temporality to investigate how overseas Chinese students made their return decisions during the COVID‐19 pandemic. Analysis of qualitative data obtained from 56 returning Chinese students during the pandemic indicates that their return decisions were relational and temporal: embedded in their familial and romantic relations and intertwined with their life trajectories of migration–education–employment. Identifying three types of return, namely hurried, predetermined, and thoughtful, during the pandemic, the study reveals the nuanced relational–temporal dynamics of the risks, opportunities, and emotions negotiated and contested between the students and their families and intimate partners during the crisis.

title: Expanding Access, Preserving Judgment: Large Language Models in Social Science Data Collection
abstract: What role should large language models (LLMs) play in social science research? The rapid rise of LLMs has generated both excitement and trepidation about their functional and ethical implications. This study evaluates their role in political science data production through the Universal Periodic Review Other Stakeholders’ Engagement (UPROSE) Dataset Project. The UPROSE project uses Universal Periodic Review reports from Non-Governmental Organizations on human rights conditions to build data on human rights and NGO engagement with international organizations. We compare LLM performance to human coders across multiple extraction tasks using established reliability metrics. LLMs perform comparably to humans for well-structured, surface-level variables but fall short in tasks requiring contextual inference or interpretive judgment. These results suggest that LLMs are best used as conditional tools that, when paired with subject-matter expertise, can expand access to high-quality data and reduce structural barriers. We conclude with best practices for hybrid workflows that enhance efficiency while maintaining interpretive quality in social science research.

title: Pave the Way to Diversion: Increased Salience of Foreign Policy at the Times of Economic Hardships
abstract: Most research on the diversionary use of force focuses on timing of conflict initiation and target selection, often treating the public as passive observers ready to take the bait. This article challenges this assumption by examining how leaders strategically elevate foreign policy issues in public discourse before resorting to the use of force. We argue that economic downturns lead to anticipatory rhetorical agenda-setting, through which leaders increase the salience of foreign policy in shaping the conditions under which military actions become feasible. Using a large language model, we measure foreign policy salience in 29,286 US presidential addresses and remarks between 1945 and 2019. Combining these data with monthly inflation and US military interventions, we examine whether patterns in presidential rhetoric are consistent with a rhetorical pathway linking economic distress to the use of force. The results are consistent with our theoretical expectation. Higher inflation is associated with increased foreign policy salience in presidential speeches and heightened salience is, in turn, associated with a greater likelihood of military intervention, while inflation itself exhibits no robust direct relationship with the use of force. Our findings align with the expectation that diversionary dynamics may unfold as a mediated process in which leaders place greater rhetorical emphasis on foreign policy issues prior to the use of force. By highlighting the role of anticipatory agenda-setting, this study offers a nuanced perspective on diversionary conflict and highlights the importance of presidential rhetoric as a key component of foreign policy outcome.

title: The Social Legacies of Repression: Family, Friends, and Political Participation
authors: Alexandra D. Blackman, Nicholas J. Lotito, Elizabeth R. Nugent, Daniel L. Tavana
abstract: Existing scholarship on the legacies of state violence treats families as the primary vehicles through which repression shapes political behavior. Yet individuals are embedded in multiple social groups; a robust literature shows that both kin and non-kin relationships are consequential for political socialization. This paper examines the comparative effects of direct repression and the repression of family members, friends, and community members on subsequent political behavior. We draw on an original nationally representative survey of 1,200 adult Tunisians, supplemented by a targeted sample of 175 sibling pairs. We find that individuals who reported themselves or family members as repressed under the Ben Ali and Bourguiba dictatorships (1956–2011) are significantly more likely to report protest participation. Those who reported repressed friends and community members are more likely to report both recent protest attendance and electoral turnout. Analyses of the sibling pairs show that the relationship between repression of friends and communities and protest participation remains significant when controlling for unobservable family characteristics. Additional analyses indicate that political discussion with friends is a key mechanism through which repression’s behavioral effects are transmitted. These findings suggest that scholars who focus on familial networks risk underestimating the broader reach of repression’s political legacies.

title: The dissent score: using events data to measure dissent when media scrutiny varies
authors: Carlisle Rainey, Harley Roe, Qing Wang, Nick Dietrich
abstract: Researchers commonly use measures of dissent or protest in their analyses. Yet a standardized, public, ready-to-use measure does not exist. In this article, we introduce such a measure—what we call the “dissent score.” To create the dissent score, we follow the standard practice in the literature and use the number of dissent events reported in events data sets. However, we make two improvements. First, we adjust for variation in media scrutiny by using the rate of dissent events—the number of dissent events compared to the total number of events reported in the data set. This is important because the total number of events explains about 50% of the variation in the number of dissent events. Second, we use a hierarchical model to partially pool these rates within and across countries. This is important because many places and times have relatively few events recorded; partially pooling reduces the measurement error. We validate the dissent score by showing that it correlates strongly with Fariss’ latent human rights protection score and substantially improves out-of-sample predictions in a reanalysis of a comprehensive model of repression. Further, while raw event counts show no support for the “more dissent in the middle” hypothesis, regime type and the dissent score have the expected inverted-U relationship. We supply the country-year dissent score for 195 countries from 1990 to 2004 in an easy-to-use format. Perhaps more importantly, we also describe our method and supply the computer code so that researchers can extend our method, make adjustments, compute the dissent score for alternative place-times, or apply the idea to new concepts. We also raise important considerations for creators of events data sets; although we focus on dissent, our approach applies broadly to any event type coded from media reports, including international conflict events and terrorism.

title: Belonging, violence, and natural resource governance: experimental evidence from Mali and Niger
authors: Alma Bezares Calderón, Simon Mercer, Ifeoluwa M Olawole, Matthew K Ribar
abstract: The presence of non-state armed groups in the Sahel complicates effective natural resource governance, which is critical for conflict resolution, economic growth, and climate resilience. In response, African governments and donor organizations have alternatively implemented both community-led and state-led interventions to strengthen natural resource governance institutions. It is unclear, however, what governance strategies will be successful in the face of these challenges. We use a vignette survey experiment administered to 3,607 rural household heads in Mali and Niger to show that (1) respondents consistently believe that a community-led natural resource governance system would be more effective, more equitable, and more resilient to climate change than either the status quo or a state-led system; (2) that members of local ethnic outgroups have greater confidence in community-led and state-led regimes relative to the status quo; and (3) exposure to violence reduces confidence in all proposed systems. This article advances our understanding of natural resource governance under institutional pluralism, explores the endogenous relationship between state capacity and armed conflict, and identifies potential limits on the extent to which strengthening local institutions can substitute for low state capacity.

title: How does political fragmentation within dominant ethnic groups shape whether challenger organizations use electoral politics, nonviolence, or violence? Evidence from Sri Lanka
abstract: How does political fragmentation within dominant ethnic groups—i.e., politically relevant ethnic groups that control the executive branch of government—impact whether challenger organizations representing politically disadvantaged ethnic groups use violence, nonviolence, or electoral politics to achieve their political goals? We know that fragmentation within politically disadvantaged groups who advocate for self-determination affects the violent and nonviolent tactics that challenger organizations use. However, ethnic mobilization is not unique to politically disadvantaged groups, and politically dominant groups may be just as fragmented as the disadvantaged groups over whom they govern. I argue that fragmentation within politically dominant ethnic groups conditions the political opportunity structures in which challenger organizations operate. As political fragmentation in the dominant group increases, creating elite divisions and leverage points, challenger organizations are more likely to use nonviolence or electoral politics, while violence becomes a tactic of last resort when these divisions are lacking. Using an original measure of political fragmentation based on legislative roll call votes in Sri Lanka, I find support for the theory. These results demonstrate that unlike fragmentation within politically disadvantaged groups, which has been found to increase the use of violence against the state, fragmentation within politically dominant ethnic groups incentivizes challenger organizations to realize their goals through nonviolent channels, lending additional insights to the literature on tactical choice in conflicts and elite divisions in social movements and nonviolent resistance.

title: Beyond coercion: how female political representation shapes sanctions termination
abstract: What explains variation in the duration of international sanctions and the mechanisms through which they are terminated? While the existing literature on sanctions termination focuses on strategic and structural factors, this study introduces a gender-based perspective, arguing that higher female political representation in the target state increases the likelihood of sanctions termination, particularly for sanctions with significant human costs. Two main pathways link women's representation to sanctions outcomes. First, women in leadership positions foster compliance with sender demands by increasing government responsiveness to humanitarian suffering and facilitating collaborative compliance processes. Second, female officeholders influence senders’ strategic calculations by signaling reforms and creating humanitarian pressure, giving senders a reason to lift sanctions. Using event history analysis on panel data of 366 sanctions cases from 1990 to 2018, the study finds that women in executive and legislative roles in target states predict shorter sanction durations, primarily through faster target compliance, while evidence for sender capitulation is more limited.

title: The legacy of rebel taxation on post-conflict fiscal capacity
authors: Andrea Arroyo Petro, Vincenzo Bove, Jessica Di Salvatore, Roberto Nisticò
abstract: Civil wars often erode state sovereignty, as institutions are replaced or co-opted by armed groups that establish informal governance structures. Among these, rebel taxation emerges as a key tool for financing wartime activities but also for administering territories. In this article, we explore whether wartime rebel taxation shapes post-conflict governments’ fiscal capacity, drawing on cross-national data from post-conflict states in Africa between 2000 and 2015. We emphasize the dual nature of rebel taxation. On the one hand, rebel taxation creates institutions and routines that may support post-conflict enforcement and compliance, especially when rebel groups are part of or co-opted into post-conflict politics. On the other hand, rebel taxation can undermine state authority by entrenching informal systems and introducing an alternative fiscal contract between citizens and non-state actors that may be hard to replace. Our analysis supports the first argument, finding a positive association between rebel taxation and post-conflict tax revenues. This result is especially pronounced in conflicts that ended without decisive military victories, suggesting that complete capitulation of rebels or governments hinders the integration of wartime taxation in post-conflict fiscal bureaucracy. Our findings highlight the enduring impact of rebel taxation on state capacity in post-conflict environments.

title: Multidimensional vulnerabilities of informal settlements in the Urban South
authors: Mingxing Chen, Wenming Song, Dadao Lu, Yu Deng, Chenglong Wang, Huiping Jiang, Yuyu Zhou, Murray W. Scown, Liangkan Chen, Jing Ma, Heran Zheng, Xuemei Bai
abstract: Informal settlements are widespread and rapidly growing, often associated with high vulnerabilities. However, global-scale understanding on their spatial distribution and complexity of vulnerability is limited. Here, we delineate the informal settlements across a sample of 1,914 cities of the Global South by integrating Sentinel-2 imagery with deep learning models, and we explore the heterogeneity of vulnerability using Urban Informal Settlement Vulnerability Index that encompasses living conditions, social infrastructure, and environmental risk. We found that Urban Informal Settlements cover 12.94 ± 2.52% of their total urban areas (approximately 34.04 × 10 3 km 2 ), especially in sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Middle Asia. Sub-Saharan African cities have the highest vulnerability of informal settlements, with 31.75 ± 6.20% of total urban areas being occupied by informal settlements, while East Asian cities exhibit relatively low vulnerability across all dimensions. We also find that urban informal settlements with high environmental exposure are widespread in the Global South, and there is a significantly polarized distribution between “low” and “high” vulnerability categories. The findings highlight the disparate distribution of multidimensional vulnerability in informal settlements across the Urban South, providing a comparative evidence base for further local assessment and context-specific policy discussions related to SDG 11.

title: Laundering and evasion in response to antislavery policies in Brazil’s cattle sector
authors: Tara Mittelberg, Marin E. Skidmore, Juliana L. S. C. Brandão, Lisa L. Rausch, Holly K. Gibbs
abstract: Modern slavery remains pervasive across many economic sectors. Progress toward eradicating it has been partially hindered by a lack of tested, comprehensive policy responses. Using data on millions of cattle transactions in Brazil, we evaluated how ranchers changed their selling behavior after being added to the “Dirty List,” a public registry that names and shames employers found to use modern slavery. Dirty Listed ranchers significantly reduced direct sales to slaughterhouses that signed sustainable supply chain commitments but evaded sanctions by laundering cattle through compliant intermediaries or selling to nonsignatory slaughterhouses. These responses weakened the financial cost of listing to ranchers, and likely allowed beef and leather linked to modern slave labor to enter international supply chains. Our findings highlight the limits of downstream enforcement and underscore the need to monitor upstream suppliers to ensure slavery-free supply chains.

title: Integrating cooperative breeding with reciprocity and culture extends Hamilton’s rule to humans
authors: Alessandra Cassar, Daniel Friedman, Shreeja Guha, Timothy Wilkins
abstract: We study how kinship and reciprocity shape giving and child care support in societies with limited access to markets. Extending Hamilton’s rule to incorporate reciprocity, we test it using behavioral data from dictator games and surveys in remote matrilocal and patrilocal villages of northeast India (N = 406 parents of young children). We replicate with data from urban Manila neighborhoods (N = 301) and the Solomon Islands (N = 624). Consistent with predictions, transfers to recipients increase with genetic relatedness to the donor and even more with relatedness to the donor’s child—a hallmark of reciprocity anchored in shared genetic investment. Nonanonymous conditions amplify giving, especially to nonkin. Cultural norms shape cooperation, but do not trump genetic relatedness. These results underscore the role of affinal ties and reciprocal exchange in sustaining cooperation, and suggest a mechanism through which cooperative breeding could contribute to the emergence of generalized reciprocity and human sociality.

title: Taylor’s law beyond finite moments: A route to dynamic financial risk
Estimating the threat of AI-agent responding across online survey platforms
authors: Grace Zhang, Robert Walatka, Stephanie Y. Chen, Alexander K. Moore, Oleg Urminsky, Kianté Fernandez, Andrea Low, Jonathan E. Bogard, Craig R. Fox
abstract: Recent research and advances in LLMs have led to widespread concern that AI agents could pose as human online survey-takers. However, it remains unclear how prevalent AI agents are on survey research platforms and how to effectively detect AI agents. We validated a series of AI detection tests that effectively separated verified-human participants from both prompted commercial and purpose-built AI agents. Using these tests, we collected surveys on seven online platforms and find wide variation in rates of respondents failing AI tests, ranging from 6 to 41% across platforms (compared to a 2.4% false-positive rate for in-person human participants). We further demonstrate that undetected AI agents can impact the results of online surveys. Our findings suggest that while there is an urgent need for AI detection tests and consistent, systematic monitoring of data quality on online platforms, some platforms currently appear to provide data with a low rate of AI agents.

abstract: Interpersonal contact is essential for cooperation and care, but it also provides a route for pathogen transmission between individuals. Hence, a key challenge for social organisms involves maintaining beneficial social contact while also limiting exposure to infection risks. Existing proposals suggest that this trade-off is guided by the interpersonal value of specific social targets. In addition, ecological and cultural factors, including historical pathogen prevalence, individualism-collectivism, tightness–looseness, and relational mobility, might also shape how people avoid pathogens. To test whether and how infection-risky social contact varies with individual-level interpersonal value and these societal-level factors, we collected data from 47,756 participants across 61 societies. Participants were randomly assigned to picture a social target - either a friend, acquaintance, stranger, or enemy. They then rated their comfort with infection-risky contact with that target (e.g., drinking from the same water bottle) and whether they would touch the target when greeting them. In all societies, participants were more comfortable with infection-risky contact and more likely to engage in physical contact during greetings with targets of higher interpersonal value. Such associations varied only modestly across societies. Notably, the associations between infection-risky contact and societal-level factors depended on target interpersonal value and were concentrated among high-value targets—contact was lower where historical pathogen prevalence and tightness were greater and higher where individualism and relational mobility were greater. These findings suggest that infection-risky contact is primarily guided by the value of social targets, with ecological and cultural factors playing a lesser role.

title: Changing contributions of emotion and reward information to learning through adolescence
authors: Camille V. Phaneuf-Hadd, Elizabeth A. Phelps, Leah H. Somerville
abstract: From childhood to adulthood, individuals’ learning and decision-making may be differentially impacted by two salient value signals for adolescents: emotions and rewards. This study superimposed these information sources to assess their independent and joint influences on learning and choice processes. Participants ages 8 to 22 y completed a reinforcement learning task, in which monetary rewards conveyed information integral to making reward-maximizing choices, while emotional expressions conveyed information incidental to this goal. In some conditions, emotion and reward invoked congruent approach-avoid tendencies; following either information source promoted making reward-maximizing (“correct”) choices. In other conditions, emotion and reward invoked incongruent approach-avoid tendencies; following the emotion cue impeded reward capture. Participants completed several measures indexing the persistence of emotion and reward information on choice and evaluations of these signals. Statistical and computational models revealed that emotion-reward incongruence hampered early learning through an incidental emotion bias on value estimates. The emotion bias decayed as reward learning progressed in adolescents and adults but endured in children. Moreover, reward-based choice increased with age across the additional measures. Although participants of all ages were initially hindered by incidental emotion cues, adults’ shift toward prioritizing integral reward outcomes indicates that goal-relevant information comes to dominate choice with age.

title: Symbolism and polarization in American public opinion: The case of border security
authors: Beth A. Simmons, Lauren E. Pinson
abstract: We explore the effect of political symbols on mass attitudes and partisan identities under conditions of political polarization. Politicians are motivated to select visible, simple, and salient symbols to influence a target audience. Some of the most potent symbols may further polarize attitudes and affect. We test our expectations using the case of border security. Two decades of polls, national panel surveys, and original conjoint experiments in the United States suggest that border barriers have become increasingly partisan over time. A final survey experiment suggests a likely mechanism: exposure to a key symbol (here, a border wall) enhances strong Republican identifiers’ nationalist attitudes. Moreover, increasing the border wall’s salience bolsters ingroup feelings among moderate Republicans and reduces strong Republicans’ warmth for Democrats (the outgroup). Political symbols that divide respondents along salient identity lines contribute to polarization, sometimes creating sharp disagreements alongside consensus in American public opinion.

title: Diffusing norms, facing friction: International non-governmental organisations and the struggle of global governance efforts
abstract: International non-governmental organisations rely on nationally embedded affiliates to advance global norms, yet relationships between headquarters and national chapters sometimes end in organisational rupture. Why do nationally embedded affiliates shift from voice to exit? This article addresses this question through a comparative study of Transparência Brasil and Uruguay Transparente, two former chapters of Transparency International (TI). Drawing on interviews, document analysis and a Most Different Systems Design, it shows that despite operating in markedly different contexts, both chapters followed a similar trajectory: persistent tensions over organisational priorities, modes of action and internal governance gradually eroded loyalty, while the absence of effective mechanisms to mediate these differences led to the disaffiliation of both chapters from TI’s network. These findings contribute to debates on the governance of international non-governmental organisations by showing how unresolved tensions between global coordination and local autonomy can lead nationally embedded affiliates to shift from voice to exit.

title: What’s the point of ideal theory?
abstract: Critics of ideal theory contend that ideal theory cannot guide present political action: from a practical point of view, they claim, social ideals are redundant at best and a positive hindrance at worst. Often the defenders of ideal theory concede these points but go on to respond that ideal theory need not be practical to have value. Both sides, however, assume that to have practical value, social ideals must be able to guide political action by serving as long-range goals or targets. I argue that this assumption is false. The point of ideal theory is not to provide guidance but rather to overcome in an ethically responsible manner the practical doubt that arises in a context of reasonable pluralism.

title: From reinvasion shock to realignment? How context and pragmatism shape far-right voting on Russia
abstract: This article provides a novel analysis of drivers of the heterogeneity in positions of European far-right parties on Russia. Concentrating on roll-call votes in the European Parliament, we theorize that due to pragmatic constraints, far-right members of European Parliament from larger domestic parties and those in government will be less likely to explicitly support Russia, expectations that are largely supported by our results. Furthermore, given that our data range from a year before the reinvasion of Ukraine in 2022 to more than 2 years after, we chart and test changes in voting over time for far-right members of European Parliament. Our theorizing and results demonstrate how electoral viability and strategic calculations constrain far-right manoeuvrers and position-taking in much the same manner as other types of political parties, therefore adding to our knowledge of far-right behaviour not simply concerning Russia but in other policy areas as well.

title: The time is now: Why talking to our children about injustice cannot wait
abstract: In this article, I argue that white parents have an obligation to have early conversations with their children about racial injustice. First, I appeal to combined considerations of fairness and solidarity. It is unfair that racial injustice exists, that Black parents cannot shield their children from knowledge of that injustice, and that acquiring that knowledge is more painful for Black children. This gives white parents solidarity-based reasons to have early injustice conversations, as a way of engaging in fate sharing with Black parents and of developing their own commitments to racial justice. Second, I argue that early conversations are required to allow white children to fulfill short-term duties to avoid causing unjust harm, avoid risking unjust harm, and stand up against injustice. Finally, I argue that beginning with conversations about justice and saving conversations about injustice for later makes it harder for children to fulfill long-term duties of justice.

title: Reply to Kettl: Public Administration and the Shifting Competing Forces of Accountability
abstract: The accountability context for how public administrators operate has shifted markedly and has become much more volatile. This shift has placed new and some conflicting demands on public administrators to demonstrate their accountability to various competing governmental actors and has complicated policy and program implementation. The changed context, its causes, and the resultant challenges are analyzed and discussed. Questions are presented for public administration research to help public administrators deal with the challenges.

title: Public Interest Capacity: The Case of Direct File
authors: Donald Moynihan, Pam Herd, Xiaoyang Xu
abstract: This article describes the conditions for creating and undermining public interest capacity, that is, the ability of the state to generate public goods with widely distributed benefits. The creation and elimination of Direct File, a free, online public tax reporting system in the United States, offers an instrumental case. The creation of Direct File depended upon political commitment sufficient to overcome private interests: both the traditional dependence on private contractors to produce digital products, and the opposition of the private tax preparation industry which saw Direct File as a competitor. Political will was not enough: creating internal capacity in the form of skilled government tech teams who could build a quality digital product was also necessary. But without this political commitment in the Trump administration, which instead pursued downsizing and was receptive to the tax preparation industry arguments, both Direct File and the team that built it were eliminated.

title: Reply to Kettl: The Field of Public Administration in America and an Unpreparedness of Its Own Making?
abstract: This Reply suggests the sub‐field of U.S.‐specific public administration is under‐prepared to address democratic deconsolidation given its multi‐decade distance from the disciplines of comparative politics and political economy and from the sub‐fields of comparative and development public administration. The narrowness of what is understand as “good” public administration by U.S.‐based scholars has largely excluded cross‐disciplinary and non‐U.S. intellectual histories which, if understood, would have deepened sub‐field intellectual depth and breadth but also, better prepared the sub‐field for America's current administrative state. This Reply suggests the value of drawing upon post‐WWII administration‐linked trends in other disciplines and upon links between administration and prior democratic deconsolidations (the U.S. is not unique). This includes the sub‐field's historical reluctance to research existential insecurity, intolerance (beyond social inequity), the role of democratic restraint, the role of crisis (or lack of) in democratic deconsolidation, and theories of democracy‐to‐autocracy and autocracy‐to‐democracy.

title: Governing Reserves: Managerial Discretion and Government Creditworthiness
authors: Sharon N. Kioko, Temirlan T. Moldogaziev
abstract: A government's ability to generate surpluses and build reserves reflects prudent financial management, with the accumulation of reserves signaling sound budgeting practices. Reserves are essential for sound fiscal governance during economic downturns, and managerial discretion over these resources is crucial to minimizing disruptions in service delivery. While the counter‐cyclical benefits of formal reserves are well documented, less attention has been paid to the discretion managers retain over reserves. Using credit ratings as a proxy for creditworthiness, we find that managerial discretion over accumulated resources enhances fiscal flexibility and strengthens creditworthiness; however, the presence of formal reserves alone does not improve credit ratings. Our study contributes to an emerging literature exploring whether better financial reporting can help us understand the critical balance between management flexibility and accountability mechanisms in public‐sector organizations.

title: Promises, Threats, and Norms: A Mixed Methods Study on Bureaucratic Support for Public Participation
authors: Jesse W. Campbell, Oscar Radyan Danar, Sanjay K. Pandey
abstract: Public participation can enhance policy quality and democratic legitimacy but may threaten bureaucratic control. We hypothesize that bureaucratic support for participation is higher when policies are less complex and participants are broadly representative. Using a mixed‐methods design involving Indonesian local public servants, we pursue complementarity by combining a 2 × 2 vignette‐based survey experiment with a Gioia analysis of qualitative reflections to explain the experimental results and further illuminate how bureaucrats evaluate participation. The experiment shows that participant representativeness significantly increases support, whereas policy complexity has no statistically significant effect. Integrating the experimental and qualitative data through joint displays reveals that bureaucrats rejecting participation frequently cite participant‐related risks, whereas supporters emphasize instrumental, procedural, and implementation benefits. Normative values, such as citizens' rights and democratic principles, are acknowledged regardless of bureaucrats' overall support. We conclude that bureaucratic support for public participation reflects how officials balance its promises, threats, and normative foundations.

title: Between the Lines: Decoding Signaling Differences in Public and Private Sector Job Advertisements
abstract: To compete in the “war for talent,” public sector employers must demonstrate advantages over private employers. While public service motivation (PSM) predicts sector preference, scholars disagree on whether public employers (can) effectively signal PSM in job advertisements. Consequently, this article examines how public and private job advertisements differ in language. We collected 5000 advertisements from both sectors and performed natural language processing (NLP) and qualitative content analysis. Both sectors use specialized language that can narrow the applicant pool. PSM signals appear more often in the public sector, but affective motives are rarely communicated; instead, self‐sacrifice is framed as a legal obligation. Public sector advertisements adopt a rational tone instead of explaining purpose and societal value. Legally mandated, saturated signals may be perceived as low‐cost and ineffective. The findings explain the mixed results concerning PSM signaling and underscore the gap between theory and practice in PSM‐related recruitment efforts.

title: Steering and Setting Free: Insights From a 20‐Year Retrospective Case Study of a Security and Justice Organization's Digital Transformation
authors: Friso Selten, Dorus van Loo, Bram Klievink
abstract: Advances in digital technologies are expected to fundamentally change how organizations operate and create value. Empirical studies show that public organizations face difficulties organizing and sustaining this digital transformation. To better understand these challenges, this study examines the organizational mechanisms underlying digital transformation in a public organization over the past 20 years. Our findings show that this transformation was primarily enabled by an emergent change approach, with influential planned changes occurring only occasionally. We identify the organizational mechanisms underlying both types of change and analyze their interdependence. Our findings suggest that both emergent and planned change approaches may be needed to enable digital transformation in public organizations effectively, but that combining them is complex in practice.

title: Quality Regulation and Competition: Evidence from Pharmaceutical Markets
authors: Juan Pablo Atal, José Ignacio Cuesta, Morten Sæthre
abstract: Quality regulation seeks to ensure quality and foster competition by reducing vertical differentiation, but it may also have adverse effects on market structure. We study this trade-off in the context of pharmaceutical bioequivalence, which is the primary quality standard for generic drugs. By exploiting the introduction of bioequivalence in Chile, we find that stronger regulation reduced the number of drugs in the market by 18% and increased average paid prices by 13%. We estimate a model of drug entry, certification, and demand to study how drug quality, aversion to generics, and certification costs shape the equilibrium effects of quality regulation. We find that quality regulation increased demand for generic drugs by resolving asymmetric information and reducing aversion to unbranded generics, which induced the entry of high-quality drugs in place of low-quality drugs. Consumer welfare increased despite higher prices and a lower number of firms. We compare minimum quality standards with alternative designs of quality regulation, including quality disclosure.

title: The Direct and Indirect Effects of Online Job Search Advice
authors: Steffen Altmann, Anita M Glenny, Robert Mahlstedt, Alexander Sebald
abstract: We study how online job search advice affects job search behavior and labor market outcomes of unemployed workers. In a large-scale field experiment embedded in the online platform of the Danish public employment service, we provide job seekers with vacancy information and occupational recommendations. Using a two-stage randomized design with regionally varying treatment intensities, we examine both direct effects of advice and treatment spillovers. We find that advice significantly increases employment and earnings when provided to a limited share of job seekers. As treatment intensity rises, these effects diminish and eventually disappear. The decline is driven by negative spillovers among treated job seekers, consistent with increased congestion in the occupations toward which job seekers redirect their search. Spillover effects on untreated job seekers are heterogeneous and depend on how advice alters occupation-specific competition in local labor markets.

title: Morality and climate policy attitudes

Evidentiary Interpretation, Discursive Injustice, and Rap on Trial
abstract: The submission of rap lyrics as inculpatory evidence (Rap on Trial) is an active prosecution tactic deployed in United States criminal trials. In this paper, I argue that interpretive ambiguity in rap lyrics is exploited in Rap on Trial cases, constituting a novel form of discursive injustice: extractive discursive injustice. Rap, a historically Black American artform, has core oral‐traditional elements such as its usage of Signifyin(g) that render it interpretably ambiguous. Utilizing the concept of hermeneutical impasses, I explain how a pernicious interpretation of rap lyrics nonetheless receives evidentiary uptake, revealing a crucial junction where injustice seeps into the courtroom. I argue that two speech act‐theoretic sites of injustice are present in Rap on Trial cases, detailing how one strain—discursive injustice—occurs. In doing so, I theorize novel forms of constitutive refusal and discursive injustice that occur when an utterance is extracted from one conversational context and deposited into another. I argue these are distinct from traditional forms in the method of arisal, though congruent with their function and display. I conclude by addressing an objection questioning the denial of truth‐telling value within rap lyrics and considering how a valid evidential use of rap lyrics might occur.

title: Integrated Explanations of Well‐Being
abstract: According to three plausible assumptions about well‐being, a person's welfare depends on (i) the valence of her experiences, (ii) the degree to which her life resonates with her, and (iii) the extent to which she fulfills her potential. Theories of well‐being have struggled to accommodate all three in a determinate manner. The difficulty can be framed as a dilemma: either jettison considered convictions, or sacrifice the clarity required for measurement and practical guidance. The aim of this article is to show that the three most influential theories are impaled by one of the horns in the dilemma, and diagnose the source of the problem. In doing so, I draw attention to an under‐theorized form of explanation that integrates phenomenological, conative and functional elements in a unified account that might overcome it.

Spatiality of preemptive coercion: How autocrats demolish informal settlements for political control
abstract: Why do authorities demolish informal settlements in metropolises? The social sciences have a long tradition of addressing this issue through the lens of economic development or welfare provision. I instead propose a theory of political control. Autocrats adopt demolition as a preemptive and coercive tool to remove communities substantively and symbolically less legible to them, thereby ensuring societal compliance and restoring visual order. Empirically, I compile a unique dataset of 320 demolished and undemolished informal settlements in Beijing between 2017 and 2018, based on satellite imagery, digital street views, and fieldwork. The results indicate that the low legibility of informal settlements to authorities correlates with a greater likelihood of demolition. This paper contributes to the social science literature by connecting legibility politics with urban governance. It also introduces a spatial perspective and leverages novel data sources to deepen our understanding of preemptive coercion under authoritarianism.

title: Human Imagery and Psychological Reactance in Persuasive Health Messages
authors: Chelsea L. Ratcliff, Helen Lillie, Manusheela Pokharel, Jakob D. Jensen, Doris E. Acheme, Benjamin Sam-Paintsil
abstract: Although mass-mediated persuasive messages often feature images of people, their impacts are surprisingly understudied. We tested whether attributes of human imagery influence psychological reactance to a health promotion PSA, either alone or combined with language style. Participants ( N = 1,100) viewed a message promoting sun safety that contained a forceful (vs. courteous) appeal and featured a model with forceful (vs. neutral) body language. The model’s physical characteristics (gender and skin tone) also varied. Both forceful text and forceful body language indirectly lowered protective behavioral intentions via reactance, and male-model messages had this effect for female participants. Our findings demonstrate the potential for features of human imagery to inadvertently hinder persuasion. Study results also highlight the value in measuring perceived visual freedom threat alongside traditional reactance measures. We discuss implications for reactance theory and measurement and highlight important directions for research on reactance to visuals.

The partisan dilemma: How people evaluate sacrificial dilemma decisions by politicians across the political divide
authors: Silvana D'Ottone, Matilde Tumino, Paul Conway
abstract: Politicians often face policy decisions where sacrificing some targets benefits others. As motivations behind such decisions can be ambiguous, partisans may ascribe nobler motives to politicians who make decisions they approve of and whose party they identify with. Consequently, evaluations of politicians can be shaped by the politician's decision, party affiliation, the domain of sacrifice, and the evaluator's political orientation. Across three studies, the US and South American participants ( N = 1595) evaluated liberal/left‐wing and conservative/right‐wing politicians who accepted or rejected educational and economic sacrifices. We examined how participants' political orientation influenced judgments of sacrificial decisions. Conservative/Right‐wing political orientation frequently (though not always) predicted higher ratings of conservative/right‐wing politicians and lower ratings of liberal/left‐wing politicians across decision acceptability, vote‐worthiness, warmth, and competence—even when both politicians made the same choice. Study 2 demonstrated that the direction of bias depends on the policy domain, with liberal‐leaning participants less accepting of educational sacrifices and more accepting of economic sacrifices than conservative‐leaning participants. Study 2 further suggested that inferences about politicians' underlying motivations partly drive partisan bias. These findings demonstrate that judgments of realistic sacrificial dilemmas are significantly influenced by the social context—specifically, who is evaluating whom and over which issues.

title: The boundaries of global concern: How socioeconomic context shapes the link between global consciousness and environmental attitudes
authors: Ayu Okvitawanli, Moh. Abdul Hakim, Reginapta Nitya Prasetyani, Takeshi Hamamura
abstract: Climate change requires unprecedented international cooperation; yet growing protectionist sentiment poses a significant barrier to collective action. Global Consciousness (GC), a psychological orientation characterized by a connection to humanity and the world as a whole, has been theorized as a key driver of benevolent behaviors, including pro‐environmental attitudes. However, empirical evidence linking GC to environmentalism remains largely confined to specific contexts, leaving the generalizability of this relationship across diverse societies unclear. Leveraging data from the European Values Survey (EVS) and the World Values Survey (WVS), this study examines the link between GC and indicators of environmentalism: confidence, active membership in environmental organizations, and prioritizing environmental protection over economic growth. We further examine whether socioeconomic context moderates this relationship, hypothesizing that the effect of GC on environmental attitudes will be stronger in wealthier nations, as measured by the Human Development Index (HDI). Multilevel models revealed that, across 35 countries in Study 1 ( N = 40,259) and 86 countries in Study 2 ( N = 123,280), GC is consistently and positively associated with environmentalism. Crucially, this relationship is significantly moderated by HDI. These results indicate that the positive effect of GC on environmentalism is stronger in countries with higher socioeconomic progress, suggesting that GC more readily translates into actions when supported by macro‐level structural resources.

title: From misogyny to mobilization: Hostile sexism and conflictual online discussions indirectly predict men's rights activism via heightened identification as a men's rights supporter
authors: Morgana Lizzio‐Wilson, Emma F. Thomas, Cassandra M. Quarisa, Anna C. Barron, Danny Osborne
abstract: Although sexism may serve as a gateway into the men's rights movement, few studies have examined group processes in online environments that fuel this reactionary movement. We address this gap by examining whether interacting with like‐minded others fosters an emergent social identity as a “men's rights supporter” among sexist men; and whether identification predicts willingness to engage in reactionary actions undermining gender equality. Across two studies ( N s = 443, 755), men completed a hostile sexism measure and read about the perceived impacts of feminism on men. Participants then either discussed whether feminism negatively impacts men in an online chatroom (group deliberation) or reflected individually (individual deliberation). Hostile sexism predicted identification as a men's rights supporter, and this link was stronger in the group deliberation condition. In turn, identification predicted greater reactionary action intentions. Unexpectedly, these effects emerged only among men who indicated that their group was unsure about the impact of feminism after the discussion. A post‐hoc content analysis of the pooled chat logs revealed that these men engaged in discussions marked by conflict and disagreement, suggesting that identification with the movement emerged through dissent rather than consensus. These findings highlight complex social dynamics underpinning engagement with the men's rights movement.

title: Egotropic and sociotropic negativity bias in social policy reform preferences
abstract: Although negativity bias is widely documented in political psychology, evidence is far more mixed when it comes to voters' preferences for social policy reform, particularly when they are confronted with trade‐offs between personal and societal outcomes. Building on existing theories of political communication, this article examines how voters evaluate policy reforms when considering realistic information about potential losses and gains. Empirically, we analyze a simu‐survey experiment examining how voters update their reform preferences in response to information derived from microsimulation modeling about the predicted effects of policy reform on their pocketbook and on the poverty level. The results show that negative information weighs more heavily than positive information in shaping reform preferences at both the egotropic and sociotropic levels. In the case of competing information, the effects are asymmetric: Positive pocketbook information tends to be neutralized by negative poverty information, whereas negative pocketbook information outweighs positive poverty information. However, egotropic negativity bias is most pronounced for smaller pocketbook losses, which are more likely to violate voters' prior expectations than larger losses. Consistent with this pattern, expectation violations—rather than differences in recall of, or trust in, information—seems the primary mechanism underlying negativity bias in policy preferences.

title: Policy Agendas in Coalition Agreements: The Enduring Influence of Policy Inheritance
authors: Gerard Breeman, Amnon Cavari, Jens Jungblut, Ilana Shpaizman, Arco Timmermans, Jon Bøe Valgermo
abstract: New governments frequently inherit issues from their predecessors, and as a result, various policy problems tend to remain on the agenda for many years. Previous research examining the role of policy inheritance has focused mainly on the agenda during a government's term in office. These studies find that because governments must first contend with the problems they inherit, there is considerably less room for new issues to emerge on the agenda. This study seeks to examine the idea of policy inheritance through the lens of coalition agreements. Coalition agreements, a feature of multiparty governments, are drafted shortly after elections and reflect the outcome of the political struggle. For this reason, one can expect that coalition agreements contain mostly issues that parties regard as important. By implication, changes in the coalition agreements' issue agenda would be a function of the political change produced by the electoral cycle, rather than of inheritance. Analyzing coalition agreements in three countries—Israel, the Netherlands, and Norway—across 42 elections, we find no evidence for this assumption. Agendas in coalition agreements do not vary with changes in the party composition of the coalition, changes in the ideological distance between parties, or changes in the party holding the office of Prime Minister. This indicates that even when new coalition governments are preparing for their term in office, inheritance remains the primary driver of agenda‐setting.

title: Partisan Wishful Thinking in Polarized Times
Voice After Exit: the Prioritization of Homeland-Facing Foreign Policy Among the Hong Kong Diaspora
authors: Maggie Shum, Eddy S. F. Yeung, Ka Ming Chan, Sanho Chung, Athena Tong, Sam Yip
abstract: Citizens around the world have migrated under the shadow of authoritarianism, and many are increasingly acquiring political and voting rights in their host countries. Yet we know little about the content of their foreign-policy preferences or the salience with which they prioritize homeland-facing issues relative to domestic concerns. We argue that experiences of authoritarian rule prior to migration generate anti-regime sentiments among diasporas, inclining them toward hawkish foreign-policy positions toward the homeland regime. These preferences heighten the salience of homeland-facing foreign policy, even relative to highly consequential domestic issues. We test this argument with harmonized candidate-choice experiments administered to an original sample of Hong Kong diasporas in four host countries (Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom, and the United States). We find that respondents strongly preferred candidates advocating hawkish economic and geopolitical policies against China. These foreign-policy positions were consistently prioritized over salient domestic issues such as healthcare and the economy, and this structure of preferences held across subgroups with varying degrees of host-country integration and homeland ties. Our findings provide novel experimental evidence that diasporas continue to care intensely about and voice on behalf of their homeland even after exit.

title: Misperceptions of Male Bias Against Female Candidates: An Obstacle to Women’s Political Representation?
authors: Carolyn Barnett, Alexandra Blackman, Marwa Shalaby

title: Relational Clientelism, Information Processing, and Accountability
abstract: Research shows that providing information on incumbent programmatic performance often has limited impact on citizen attitudes towards incumbents, even if citizens tend to care strongly about corruption and service delivery. We use a survey experiment in South Africa and Tunisia to study if relational clientelism, a type of clientelism often valued by clients, plays a role in this puzzle. We present respondents with a radiocast that varies the profile of the politician (clientelistic vs. neutral) and his performance in service delivery and corruption (good vs. bad). We find that, when clientelistic politicians are valued, performance information on them matters less than for neutral politicians. The effect appears to operate via motivated reasoning: Respondents are less likely to process negative performance information when exposed to the clientelistic profile. Our findings suggest that, in certain contexts, relational clientelism is a valued candidate characteristic that can offset bad programmatic performance akin to co-partisanship or co-ethnicity.

title: Conversation Without Conversion: Evidence from Cross-Partisan Interactions on a Mobile Chat Platform
Daughters and Political Preferences of Politicians: A Preregistered Prospective Study on Swedish Politicians
authors: Anna Dreber, Magnus Johannesson, Elin Naurin, Patrik Öhberg
abstract: Important studies have suggested that politicians become more liberal by having daughters, but more recent work has been unable to replicate this result. It is therefore essential to further clarify how politicians’ family situations affect their policy making in different contexts, and in particular when it comes to gender-related policies. We provide a unique test based on prospective data collection on Swedish politicians based on a pre-analysis plan strictly followed in all analyses and tests. Data is collected in two surveys implemented after the 2022 general parliamentary election in Sweden on members of parliament and candidates in the parliamentary election (n=1,147 complete responders are included in our analyses). In our primary hypotheses, we test whether having daughters is associated with more left-leaning political preferences, a stronger preference for female-favoring policies, and a weaker preference for male-favoring policies. We find no evidence of an effect on left-leaning political preferences or female-favoring policies. These results do not support the original work on this topic but are in line with the more recent null results. We also find suggestive evidence (p<0.05) that having daughters is associated with a weaker preference for male-favoring policies. As the effects of having daughters on male-favoring policies have not been explored earlier, this opens up an interesting avenue to investigate in future studies.

title: Culture Holds us Together: Confucian Clan Culture and Collective Actions in China’s Land Expropriation
Migration Studies and International Business Scholarship: Toward Mutual Renewal in the Study of High-Skilled Migration
authors: Aida Hajro, Milda Žilinskaitė, Francisco D. Bretones
abstract: This article introduces a special issue of International Migration Review , aimed at bringing migration studies and international business (IB) scholarship into dialogue. Although both interdisciplinary fields examine processes that are fundamentally interconnected—the movement of people and the movement of firms—they have largely developed in parallel. In this introduction, we review the most relevant IB scholarship, consider the extent to which it has drawn on migration-related insights, and reflect on why it has nonetheless remained relatively detached from broader migration studies. We then examine what IB can contribute to research on high-skilled migration, what migration studies can offer IB in return, and outline four pathways for building stronger conceptual bridges between the two fields. Collectively, the articles in this special issue illustrate that potential by illuminating the multiple intersections between high-skilled migration and IB.

title: Fragile Transnationalism: Rethinking Migrant Transnationalism for a Post-Neoliberal World
abstract: In this article, we develop the concept of fragile transnationalism to conceptualize the re-infrastructuring of migrant transnationalism under conditions of post-neoliberal globalization. Since the 2008 Great Recession, the world has witnessed the demise of neoliberal globalization, amid an ongoing political, socioeconomic, and environmental polycrisis, and the consequent emergence of a post-neoliberal world order. We argue that the attendant fragmentation of global political order, the resurgence of authoritarian nationalism worldwide, and the societal implications of climate change and emergencies have reconfigured the basic conditions for migrant transnationalism. Our analysis points to a far-reaching reassertion of the nation-state in migration governance. In response, we retheorize migration infrastructure as a conceptual lens for analyzing migrant transnationalism. We reveal how an assemblage of weak infrastructures, particularly the fragility within and between its constituent components, has reshaped the logic, practice, and experiences of transnational migration and lives.

title: Book Review: Now We Are Here OliveiraG. (2025). Now We Are Here: Family Migration, Children’s Education, and Dreams for a Better Life. Stanford University Press. 250 Pages, $110.00 Hardcover
Spillover effects of a far-left populist's victory: Revisiting the 1998 Venezuela election
Hiring on education specificity across careers: evidence from a factorial survey experiment with employers in Germany and England
abstract: Prior observational research suggests that at the beginning of their careers, workers benefit from having specific education, as education that is closely linked to specific jobs. These relative payoffs to educational specificity, however, decline across the life-course. One central explanation for this is on the employer side: for late-career candidates, employers may perceive specific qualifications as a signal of outdated and inflexible skills. In this paper, we draw on novel data from a factorial survey experiment conducted with employers in Germany and England, to examine whether evaluations of specific education differ for early and late-career candidates. Moreover, we investigate the potential explanatory role of working and training histories. Our results show wide preferences for specific education over more general education, and this preference is strikingly similar for early and late-career candidates in the two countries. Still, for early-career candidates in Germany, we found particularly high evaluations of specificity for candidates with vocational training as compared to university graduates. Moreover, for late-career candidates, our results suggest that hiring agents differently value specificity in the two countries: in Germany, relevant work experience comes with a smaller specificity premium, whereas in England, on-the-job training can compensate for specific education.

title: Feasible GLS for time series regression
Strategic alienation: The dynamics of group appeals in negative campaigning
abstract: This paper examines how political parties use social group appeals in negative campaigning. We argue that parties strategically target opponents with group-based attacks to portray them as failing key social groups. Using a novel dataset of Facebook and Twitter posts by parties in the UK (2016–2024), linked to voter perceptions of group representation from the British Election Study, we test whether such attacks are more likely when the sender party enjoys strong group-based credibility, or the target party is seen as a weak representative of the respective group, or both. We find no evidence for the former but strong support for the latter: parties disproportionately target rivals with poor reputations for representing specific groups, and especially so when the sender holds a reputational advantage. These findings advance our understanding of identity-driven party competition, showing that group-based attacks exploit opponents’ representational vulnerabilities rather than reinforce attackers’ own strength.
