title: Recognizing Indigenous peoples
Skill and spatial mismatches for sustainable development in Brazil
authors: Anna K. Berryman, Fernanda Senra de Moura, Joris Bücker, Pete Barbrook-Johnson, Marek Hanusch, Penny Mealy, J. Doyne Farmer, R. Maria del Rio-Chanona
abstract: Deforestation is a major source of global greenhouse gas emissions, and continued forest loss risks pushing the Amazon from a carbon sink to a carbon source. While recent work shows that productivity-led structural transformation towards less land-intensive sectors can reduce deforestation, the labour market implications of such pathways remain poorly understood. Here we address this gap by developing a spatially and occupationally explicit agent-based labour market model informed by empirically observed job-transition networks to simulate the ability of workers to respond to labour demand shocks. Our analysis reveals significant skill and geographic mobility frictions that constrain workers’ ability to adapt to structural change. Applying the model to productivity-driven development scenarios, we find that pathways delivering the largest deforestation and emission reductions disproportionately benefit high-skill workers while increasing unemployment among agricultural and other low-skill workers. Mobility-enhancing labour market policies can mitigate these effects, highlighting the importance of understanding labour market dynamics for equitable and feasible deforestation-reducing development pathways.

title: Quantifying assets for the geopolitics of climate change mitigation
authors: Guanna Pan, Ulrike Kornek, Chen Chris Gong, Edna Johanna Molina Bacca, Gunnar Luderer, Ottmar Edenhofer
abstract: Climate change mitigation reshapes the distribution of economic assets in the low-carbon transition. Here we quantify climate-related assets for 169 countries across four dimensions: fossil fuel production, climate change damages, renewable energy potential and land carbon sequestration capacity. We combine integrated assessment models, climate projections, economic damage functions and biosphere datasets to assess asset changes under multiple mitigation scenarios. Geopolitical challenges and opportunities arise from climate change mitigation because losses and gains across energy and environmental assets are country-specific, which we further characterize through a broad clustering and a detailed pairwise similarity analysis. Our analysis suggests comparatively moderate impacts for the USA, the European Union and China, highlighting the challenge that the largest economic powers may not be those with the strongest asset-based interest for climate action. While our framework remains limited, our data provide input for integrating other ethical, governance and socioeconomic factors in future analyses of opportunities and challenges for ambitious climate change mitigation.

title: Entailment and implicature in the language of thought
authors: Irene Canudas Grabolosa, Luca Lorenzo Bonatti, Gennaro Chierchia
abstract: Human language processing involves constant computation of entailments and implicatures, yet the extent to which these inferences depend on linguistic communication remains unclear. This study investigates whether logical structures akin to those in natural language can be derived from purely visual input. Specifically, we examine the polarity sensitivity of scalar inferences (SIs) in non-linguistic contexts. Prior research has established that SIs are preferentially computed in Upward Entailing (UE) rather than Downward Entailing (DE) environments, and we extend those studies by examining whether this pattern extends to visual conceptualization. We conducted three experiments using an oddball paradigm with minimal instructions to our participants, where they witenessed animated ball collisions. Across studies, participants consistently detected these changes to the quantified structure of events (changes from some to all) more readily in UE than in DE conditions, mirroring SI patterns observed in language. These findings suggest that the conceptualization of visual scenes parallels linguistic representations, implying that entailment relations are not exclusive to communication but emerge naturally from cognitive structures. Our results support grammaticalized theories of implicatures, challenging traditional Gricean views that implicatures stem solely from communicative intent. This work contributes to ongoing debates on the relationship between language and thought, demonstrating that logical inferences can arise independently of linguistic input.

title: Buying Books, Buying Diversity? Public Procurement Theory and the Brazilian State as Book Buyer
authors: Marcel Felipe Machado Lopes, Paula Roméro Cajaty Lopes
abstract: Governments are among the largest single buyers of books, yet public procurement research rarely asks what state purchasing does to the diversity of the market it buys from. This article examines federal book procurement in Brazil using item-level electronic invoice (NF-e) data published by the Office of the Comptroller General (CGU). The data cover 60 months between October 2021 and September 2026 and R$21.9 billion in purchases, 96.7% of which were made by a single buyer, the National Fund for Education Development (FNDE). Drawing on Stirling's variety–balance–disparity framework, we build five indicators of bibliodiversity: supplier concentration (Herfindahl–Hirschman index), the share of the four and eight largest suppliers, supplier evenness, title evenness, and territorial inequality among suppliers. The results describe a market with high variety but low balance. A median of 280 suppliers invoice the federal government each month, yet the four largest take a median 68% of value, and two publishers, FTD and Moderna, account for 45% of the whole series. Concentration is episodic rather than trending: 13 of 60 months exceed the HHI threshold of 2,500, with no significant monotonic trend. Territorial inequality is extreme and stable (median Gini 0.93), with São Paulo-based emitters taking 93% of value. Title diversity falls when supplier concentration rises (Spearman ρ = −0.61) and has declined sharply since mid-2025. We read these patterns against transaction cost, principal–agent, competition, strategic-procurement and institutional theories. We argue that, in markets for unique cultural goods purchased without price competition, the locus of competition moves from the tender to the pre-selection stage, so programme design rather than tendering rules becomes the main lever for diversity. We derive five propositions and discuss the data-quality limits of invoice-based procurement analytics.

title: Compensatory Input Versus Unequal Gains: Why Schooling Does Not Necessarily Equalize Socioeconomic Achievement Gaps
abstract: Recent research has failed to provide clear-cut evidence that schooling equalizes social gaps in achievement. This stands at odds with the dominant view of compensatory input, which holds that even unequal schooling equalizes learning because it compensates for the even more unequal learning inputs children would receive in its absence. I test the previously neglected mechanism of unequal gains from schooling, which could counteract compensatory input and thus explain why studies often fail to find equalization. The unequal gains hypothesis posits a Matthew effect whereby learning gains from schooling depend on children’s prior skills, so that students from higher (lower) socioeconomic backgrounds benefit more (less) from schooling because of their, on average, higher (lower) skills at school entry. Because both mechanisms can operate simultaneously, assessing the equalizing power of schooling requires accounting for achievement prior to schooling. Using data from the newborn cohort of the German National Educational Panel Study (NEPS), I first replicated earlier findings from Germany on the beneficial but non-equalizing effects of school exposure on student achievement—scientific literacy and vocabulary—in Grade 1. Second, after accounting for children’s achievement before schooling, I found evidence of unequal gains counteracting equalization; net of these unequal gains, school exposure did level out learning gaps by social background, although only in the domain of scientific literacy. The findings underline the importance of incorporating prior achievement into studies of school equalization.

title: Flourishing and Health in Kenya. Philosophical Perspectives and Empirical Insights.
abstract: Numerous studies have demonstrated positive associations between broader dimensions of wellbeing and health. However, evidence from Kenya on this association is scarce and mostly focused on broad evaluative measures of wellbeing, such as life satisfaction. This study draws on conceptualizations of wellbeing from Sub-Saharan African philosophical literature as motivation for examining various specific dimensions of wellbeing in the Global Flourishing Study and analyzing their association with subsequent health in Kenya as a case study, using a longitudinal panel design. Data were drawn from waves 1 (2023; n=11389 individuals) and 2 (2024; n= 7698 individuals) of the Global Flourishing Study. The data are representative of the general population in Kenya. Linear regression models with a lagged dependent variable are used to test the association of wave 1 wellbeing indicators with subsequent physical and mental health at wave 2. The findings indicate that several dimensions of wellbeing - including livelihood security, satisfaction with personal relationships, meaning and purpose, agency and freedom to pursue what is most important in life - are positively associated with subsequent self-rated physical and mental health in Kenya.

title: The Impact of U.S. Tariffs on European Public Opinion: Evidence From a Natural Experiment
abstract: How do tariff escalations shape public attitudes in targeted countries? This registered report examines how the second Trump Administration's April 2025 tariff escalation affected European public opinion. Leveraging the announcement's timing during the fieldwork of Standard Eurobarometer 103.3 as an unexpected event, I compare respondents interviewed before and after. Drawing on theories of external threat, in-group identity, and cooperative reciprocity, I test whether the escalation strengthened pro-EU sentiment, worsened views of the United States, and shifted cooperation preferences. I find that it reduced favorable views of the United States, while effects on EU attachment and cooperation preferences were small and non-significant. The decline in favorable views of the United States is concentrated in the most negative response category, indicating that negative views intensified. These results suggest that economic threats from an ally can sharpen antagonism toward the threatening actor without producing broad in-group consolidation or shifts in trade cooperation preferences.

title: Silicon Ethics: Comparing the Dynamics of Human and LLM Responses to Ethical Dilemmas
abstract: A key element in alignment research is commonly captured by the phrase “alignment with human values.” Human ethical judgment, however, is plural, unstable, affectively charged, socially embedded, and often justified after the fact. This article proposes a systematic comparative methodology emphasizing the potential complementarity of how human and silicon ethics may differ. Drawing on literature of moral psychology, it identifies five dynamics of human ethical judgment systematically comparing them with their functional analogues in generative models. The goal is not to anthropomorphize LLMs or treat human judgment as a gold standard, but to compare the latent structures of the dynamics in vivo and in silico. The article argues that such comparison can extend alignment research beyond mimetic reproduction of human preferences toward compensatory intelligence: AI systems that help humans notice neglected consequences, test consistency, consider alternative moral frames, and deliberate more responsibly about their own commitments.

title: Digital capacity in Brazilian municipalities: fiscal autonomy, bureaucratic structure and heterogeneity
abstract: Over the past decades, digital transformation has become a central aspect of state modernization. In this article, we treat this process as a form of state capacity building — specifically, of the digital capacity of the state. Our aim is to assess whether, at the municipal level, fiscal capacity and bureaucratic quality account for higher levels of digital capacity. To this end, we adapt to the municipal context a concept originally formulated for national states and construct the Municipal Digital Capacity Index (ICDM), a novel and comprehensive measure built from the seven waves of the Brazilian Survey of Basic Municipal Information (MUNIC) that include an information and communication technology module between 2004 and 2024, covering virtually all Brazilian municipalities in each wave. Using the ICDM as the dependent variable, we estimate panel models designed to recover between-municipality effects. Fiscal autonomy is the strongest determinant of digital capacity, with a magnitude far exceeding that of bureaucratic attributes, whose effects are positive but modest. None of these effects, however, operates uniformly: own-source revenue yields more in low-income municipalities, staff qualification pays off only where there is organizational structure to absorb it, and the share of politically appointed staff, whose average effect is null, is positive in poorer municipalities and negative in wealthier ones.

title: Mistrust the State, Trust the Market Mass Investing Culture with Postsocialist Flavour
abstract: In this paper, I aim to make sense of the meanings surrounding the recent surge in popularity of non-professional investing in the Czech and Slovak postsocialist context. The research is based on interviews with individual retail investors and fieldwork conducted at various investor events, meet-ups, and conferences. My Czech and Slovak research partners view investing as a means to ensure the long-term continuation of their household’s wealth and security. Being invested then represents a certain hedge against the growing inaccessibility of housing and the cost-of-living crisis. My interviewees entrust what Giddens calls ontological security to institutions of global capitalism rather than to local state systems. The shift in trust remains embedded in distinctly postsocialist moral framing, proclaiming a more ethical, self-responsible, and rational type of household financial management, which aligns with the core moral imperative of mass investment culture – everybody should invest. Conversely, welfare-state-based alternatives face generalized distrust as unreliable.

title: A Sociolinguistic Inquiry into Vietnamese Swearing: Regional Variation and Cross-Cultural Parallels
abstract: This exploratory, pilot-scale study investigates the Vietnamese swearing construction built from an obscene verb, a kinship term and a second-person pronoun (địt mẹ mày, đụ má mày 'fuck your mother', mả cha mi 'your father's grave') through two questions: how kin-directed swearing differs across regions and which part of the construction reveals the speaker's region (RQ1); and why Vietnamese swearing targets kin and women, viewed against the full repertoire of swearing themes in Vietnamese and neighbouring languages (RQ2). It combines eight Vietnamese dictionaries (1651–2021) and comparative dictionaries of Mường, Cham, Teochew and Cantonese with an online convenience-sample survey of 50 young speakers across four regions, a small Quốc ngữ prose corpus, and a thematic comparison with ten other language communities. For RQ1, the dictionaries show no regional boundary in the verb before 1931, whereas the survey finds a clear North/South split in both the verb and the word for "mother"; regional information is asymmetric, with Southern and Central forms acting as strong markers while standard-compatible forms (địt, mẹ) and online abbreviations (đm, vkl) spread across all regions. For RQ2, sex and kin dominate the free lists; the mother-directed sexual formula occurs in Vietnamese, Chinese, Thai, Hindi and English but is absent from Japanese, so it cannot be attributed to Confucian heritage alone. Kin-directed swearing is rated more offensive than self-directed swearing and triggers more active responses; swears that deny the hearer's descent (đồ con hoang, cả họ nhà mày) are the heaviest and the least mitigated among friends. Young respondents name affection for kin, not family face, as the main reason; we read this as a contemporary synchronic reinterpretation of templates whose diachronic origin lies in honour-based lineage norms. Taken together, the target of kin-directed swearing is the hearer's legitimate standing within the lineage. Results describe young, internet-using speakers and should be read as hypothesis-generating.

title: Standpoint Theory and the Enactment of the Social Relation of Comradeship through Social Research
abstract: This paper discusses the ethico-political impetus for seeking to establish the social relation of comradeship with socially marginalised research participants of projects concerned with social justice and countering structural oppression. To this end, the paper explores Olufemi O. Táíwò’s (2020) distinction between liberal and constructive approaches to Standpoint Theory, before considering the social relations of allyship and comradeship through the context of a project that examined structural disablement and precarious work in the UK. In light of this analysis, I call on other social researchers to consider the necessity of enacting the social relation of comradeship with socially marginalised participants as a way of affirming mutual recognition, strengthening emancipatory research, and producing socially useful dialogic knowledge.

title: Impact of Social Media Platforms on Youth: An Anthropological Study
abstract: Social media has become a ubiquitous sociocultural phenomenon, transforming how young people communicate, socialize, and construct identities. This anthropological study examines social media use among young people aged 18–25 in urban and semi-urban areas of Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, South India. It explores usage patterns, self-identity expression, maintenance of social relationships, digital literacy, and the influence of gender, education, and socioeconomic background on digital participation. It also considers how young people perceive social media’s everyday effects on their social and cultural lives. A mixed-methods design was adopted. Quantitative data were collected through a questionnaire administered to 60 youth respondents, while semi-structured interviews were conducted with 10 participants. The questionnaire demonstrated high overall reliability (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.91), and its individual scales showed acceptable to high reliability. Content validity was reviewed by experts, while exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses were used to assess construct validity. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests of independence; qualitative data were analyzed thematically using NVivo. Findings indicate that social media is embedded in young people’s everyday lives: 73.3% reported using platforms more than once daily. WhatsApp (93.3%), Instagram (88.3%), and YouTube (81.7%) were the most widely used platforms. Entertainment (90.0%) and maintaining contact with friends (85.0%) were the leading purposes, followed by information seeking (63.3%) and identity expression (35.0%). Digital literacy levels were low for 23.3% of respondents, medium for 48.3%, and high for 28.3%. Differences were particularly evident in advanced skills, including evaluating information and managing privacy. Hypothesis testing found significant associations between digital literacy and frequency of use (p = 0.048; Cramér’s V = 0.324), digital literacy and platform diversity (p = 0.047; Cramér’s V = 0.283), gender and identity expression (p = 0.037; Cramér’s V = 0.331), and gender and platform choice (p = 0.041; Cramér’s V = 0.326). Other hypothesized relationships were not statistically significant. The qualitative analysis identified five themes: curated identity performance, digital kinship and connectivity, stratified digital competencies, gendered digital surveillance, and ambivalent impression perceptions. The study contributes to digital anthropology by illustrating how global platforms are locally adopted in South Indian contexts, how social relationships are sustained in digital spaces, and how digital literacy may function as cultural capital. It offers recommendations for educators, parents, policymakers, platform designers, and young people to promote more equitable and beneficial digital participation.

title: Instrument Revision and False Change in Repeated Surveys: A Typology and Diagnostic Protocol for Secondary Users
abstract: Repeated surveys revise their instruments between rounds and document each revision item by item. Such documentation records what changed but not what the change does to a trend, so secondary users can mistake an instrument effect for change in the population. This article proposes a typology that classifies revisions by their consequence for the information in the released data (removal, redistribution, stimulus change, and misidentification), links each type to its identification status and remedy, and puts it into practice through a five-step diagnostic protocol: comparing source instruments, screening against a reference distribution of unmodified trend items, classifying the revision, choosing an estimand, and auditing metadata. Applied to the 2024 European Working Conditions Survey, the protocol shows that a filter and a self-labeling question placed before the discrimination battery leave the 2015 to 2024 contrast identified only as a lower bound; six of seven grounds fell below every unmodified reference item, and the observed decline would be real only if the new instrument retained more than 60 percent of reports. A new cyberbullying item redistributed reports from the adjacent bullying item, and the data bound the comparable change between odds ratios of 0.75 and 0.98. Changes in item order and response coding left a pace-of-work battery unresolved, while a minor stem change produced no detectable break. The metadata audit found nine variables labeled with the stem of a different question, in both data editions, and a harmonized trend variable that omits one of the two items its label combines. Comparability should be established from the source instruments and the released data before substantive analysis begins.

title: Remembering without institutions: legal-political memory, oral transmission, and diaspora identity among Kurds in Turkey and Europe
abstract: Drawing on 80 interviews across three sub-samples — the Kurdish-majority region of Turkey (n=25), Central Anatolia (n=25), and the European diaspora (n=30) — this article examines how legal-political memory of forced displacement is transmitted across generations. Using an inductively developed 11-category thematic coding framework, we find a sharp geographic gradient in informal oral transmission (64% Region, 40% Central Anatolia, 16.7% diaspora), with an inverse rise in institutional/archival memory in the diaspora (50%, versus 16–20% in Turkey; suggestive rather than conclusive once corrected for multiple comparisons). Spatial displacement is narrated concretely in the region of origin but gives way, in the diaspora, to an abstract negotiation of layered belonging. We suggest that memory transmission without institutional archives relies on embodied domestic channels vulnerable to migration's ruptures — a vulnerability diaspora communities compensate for through new institutional infrastructures rather than reconstruction. The article offers a comparative, exploratory account of how a stateless-nation diaspora reconstructs continuity across ruptured contexts.

title: Visual Resistance Assemblages: Recurring Multimodal Configurations in Kenya’s Gen Z Finance Bill Protests
abstract: Social-media protest communication is increasingly multimodal, combining language, imagery, typography, sound, performance and platform-specific features. While existing research has demonstrated how such resources produce meaning within individual artefacts and genres, comparatively less attention has been given to how functionally related multimodal configurations recur across heterogeneous artefacts within the same protest corpus. This study addresses this corpus-level problem through a qualitative multimodal analysis of 72 protest artefacts published or circulated on X during Kenya’s June–July 2024 Finance Bill protests, analysed through multimodal social semiotics and cross-artefact comparison. The analysis identifies five recurring configurations: Constitutional Legitimation, Distributed Agency, Comparative Fiscal Information Design, Visual Witnessing and Collective Identity, and Satirical Recontextualization. These configurations are not treated as mutually exclusive artefact categories; rather, they represent recurring relationships among heterogeneous semiotic resources that retain comparable communicative functions despite variation in genre and surface realisation. The study proposes the concept of Visual Resistance Assemblages (VRA) as a descriptive analytical unit for identifying such corpus-level recurrence. The findings demonstrate how constitutional discourse, distributed participation, comparative fiscal reasoning, collective representation and satirical recontextualisation were organised through heterogeneous multimodal resources. VRA complements existing multimodal, assemblage-oriented and digital activism approaches by shifting attention from multimodality within individual artefacts to recurring multimodal organisation across protest corpora.

title: The Emotional Meaning and Sociocultural Implications of 'Eojunggan-hada' in Korean Society: An Exploratory Study
abstract: This study explores how the Korean expression 'eojunggan-hada' (being in-between) extends beyond simple linguistic ambiguity to reflect issues of personal identity and social belonging. Unlike previous Korean linguistics research that focused on linguistic ambiguity and mitigation expressions, this study defines 'eojunggan-hada' as a way of being positioned at the boundaries of identity and belonging, analyzing its sociocultural implications. A survey of 111 respondents revealed that participants frequently experience being in-between in daily life (mean 3.44), perceiving it more as a product of social structural conditions (mean 3.46) rather than personal character traits (mean 3.22). Notably, daily experience of in-betweenness showed a strong positive correlation with attributing it to one's personality (r = .64, p < .001), suggesting that the more frequently people feel in-between, the more they blame their own character for it. Qualitative analysis of open-ended responses confirmed that being in-between functions simultaneously as discomfort and survival strategy. This study conceptualizes 'eojunggan-hada' as a boundary emotion formed within Korea's unique collectivist culture and relational pressures, proposing that it represents not individual indecisiveness but rather a way of existence created by social structures.

title: Automated Essay Scoring with GPT Models: A Comparison with Human Ratings of IEP Written Products
abstract: This study explores the integration of Large Language Model (LLM)-based Automated Essay Scoring (AES) into classroom writing assessment within an Intensive English Program (IEP). Using a corpus of 46 multi-draft capstone essays written by international students in an Academic Literacies course, the study evaluates the performance of two OpenAI models (GPT-4.1-mini and GPT-5.1) against rubric-based human instructor scores. Essays were scored twice by each model under controlled temperature settings to evaluate linear association, systematic bias, inter-model consistency, and performance-band agreement. Findings reveal that while both LLM scores maintain moderate positive correlations with human ratings (r = .44 for GPT-4.1-mini; r = .49 for GPT-5.1), both models exhibit systematic negative bias, scoring essays an average of 13 points lower than the human instructor. However, the two models demonstrate strong inter-model consistency (r = .84) and an exact band-level agreement of 87%. Qualitative analysis of the holistic comments shows that LLMs focus on global discourse features but lack sensitivity to local, process-oriented classroom constructs. The results suggest that uncalibrated zero-shot LLMs serve better as formative diagnostic tools than autonomous grading systems. Keywords: Automated essay scoring, Large Language Models, GPT-5, L2 academic writing, multi-method validity, formative assessment.

title: Globalization Unravelling? ASML and the Geopolitics of Europe-China Tech Decoupling
authors: Naná de Graaff, Jaša Veselinovič, Tyler, A.G. (Adam Geoffrey)
abstract: This article investigates the geopolitical dynamics driving Europe’s emerging technological decoupling from China. Focusing on the semiconductor industry and the Dutch semiconductor firm ASML, it examines how technonationalism emanating from the US has shaped a small European member state’s policy response amid intensifying US-China rivalry. The article analyses how national security arguments and US strategic influence aimed at undermining China’s advances in high-tech has reshaped the Dutch semiconductor export control regime in a way that seemingly contradicts both ASML’s corporate interests and Dutch long-term economic interests. Moreover, cutting the dependency ties of China to one of the few chokepoint industries and tech firms in the EU arguably undermines its commitment to ‘technological sovereignty’. We explain these puzzling outcomes through the inherent contradictions within technonationalism and the tensions between state and corporate actors strategizing around different national security and profit-oriented interests. As such, we argue that the case of ASML offers a useful prism through which to study the ongoing ‘geoeconomic’ shift in the global political economy in which the alignment of the geopolitical and capital logics characteristic of neoliberal globalisation is coming apart, with state and corporate actors attempting to realign these logics into different configurations.

title: Manufactured Desire： How Social Media and Influencer Agencies Sexualise and Monetise Pregnant Influencers
abstract: This article examines how pregnant influencers on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, are sexualised and monetised through the interlocking practices of the platform, influencer agencies and influencers themselves. Taking the 2024 controversy around the appearance influencer YīLìXiǎoShāZi and the # 孕妇摇 (Pregnancy Swing Dance) challenge as its point of departure, the study combines visual analysis of top-ranked Douyin posts, in-depth interviews with an influencer, an influencer agency employee and a platform employee, and sentiment analysis of 4,874 user comments. This article interprets platform monetisation structures and influencer agency production routines as organising influencers’ embodied labour into standardised production roles and measurable commercial attributes. It proposes the “factory of desire” as a framework for understanding how platforms, influencer agencies and influencers mutually enable and constrain the commodification of pregnant bodies. Interviewees described unwritten rules through which sexualised content can remain visible under mainland China's restrictions on pornography: perceived emphasis on skin exposure in automated moderation, a grey zone known as 擦边 (cābiān, "skirting the boundary"), and appeals framed around "pregnancy beauty". The analysis suggests that these commercial and regulatory conditions can encourage pregnant influencers to reproduce porn chic conventions, while constraining their subsequent commercial options. Within the sampled comments on videos criticising the sexualisation of pregnancy, disgust had the highest average model score; these findings describe this selected discussion rather than public opinion as a whole.

title: Decolonising Water Diplomacy: Concepts, Debates, and Practice
abstract: Water diplomacy is commonly presented as a practical response to tensions over shared waters. It brings together negotiation, technical expertise, international water law, basin institutions, and practices of cooperation and peacebuilding. Yet the terms through which water diplomacy is often organised — security, cooperation, neutrality, development, expertise, and peace — are not politically innocent. They are shaped by histories of empire, unequal treaties, colonial borders, geopolitical asymmetries, donor agendas, and knowledge hierarchies. This article introduces decolonising water diplomacy as an emerging orientation that does not reject diplomacy, law, science, or cooperation, but asks how their assumptions, procedures, and outcomes are historically produced. It defines water diplomacy, situates it in relation to water security, water peace, critical hydropolitics, water justice, and decolonial thought, and explains what a decolonial perspective adds in practice. The article argues that decolonising water diplomacy does not simply add justice to existing approaches; it asks how peace, security, and cooperation are defined, whose histories and knowledges they privilege, and how they might be reworked toward historical responsibility, epistemic justice, recognition, dignity, and more accountable forms of peace.

title: Generalised Conversational Implicature in Kenyan Generation Z Digital Protest Discourse: Q-, I-, and M-Heuristics in the 2024 Finance Bill Protests on X
authors: Castro Chebukosi, Bernard Kodak, Jane Ombati
abstract: The June–July 2024 Finance Bill protests in Kenya produced a distinctive corpus of digitally mediated political communication in which Gen Z-associated protesters on X (formerly Twitter) relied on omission, shared background knowledge and stylistic markedness to construct political meaning beyond the literal content of their posts. This study examines how such strategies generated Generalised Conversational Implicature (GCI), applying Levinson’s (2000) Q-, I-, and M-heuristic framework to a purposively sampled corpus of 72 protest artefacts retrieved from X in June 2026. Using thematic and pragmatic coding, the analysis shows that condensed slogans, mobilisation language and constitutional citation generated Q-heuristic implicatures through informational economy; shared political, cultural and generational knowledge generated I-heuristic implicatures; and marked linguistic, visual and performative choices generated M-heuristic implicatures, extending Levinson’s lexical account of markedness into a multimodal register. The three heuristics frequently layered within single artefacts, and thematic coding further revealed six protest-specific inferential patterns beyond Levinson’s original typology: anti-co-optation, constitutional-sovereignty, trauma-memory, care-based, data-activism and digital-network patterns. The study demonstrates how GCI analysis can be extended to fast-paced, multimodal, digitally networked political communication when its categories are made explicit and their limits are clearly bounded.

title: Modeling Cooperation as Information Flow: Ripple Structures and Behavioral Digital Twins
abstract: Recent advances in articial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models, have signicantly improved performance in language understanding, vision, and reasoning. How- ever, a fundamental limitation remains: current AI systems still lack an explicit under- standing of the logical structure by which humans make decisions within specic situations and relationships. This limitation is not merely a shortage of intelligence, but a missing layer of context-dependent decision logic. This study proposes a theoretical framework and methodological protocol that redenes human cooperation as an observable information ow rather than a psychological or moral phenomenon. We model cooperative propagation as Ripple structures, which are directional causal chains of actions in which A helps B and B in turn helps C, and we introduce the concept of a Behavioral Digital Twin, dened as a map- ping of decision logic derived from situation, relationships, and action history. We further present a non-interventional observational protocol for capturing naturally occurring coop- erative behaviors through naturalistic observation environments, and outline a validation framework for future empirical work. All behavioral events remain voluntary; the proto- col introduces observation infrastructure without prescribing or incentivizing actions. All gures and examples in this manuscript are conceptual illustrations intended to clarify the- oretical constructs. This work aims to provide a foundational layer connecting AI research, social systems research, and Web3 governance.

title: Accountability Gap Behind Predatory Publishing in Philippine Academia
abstract: The mandate of the Philippines’ Commission on Higher Education ties faculty promotion in state universities and colleges to research publications. This commentary argues that the policy's emphasis on publication volume, unmatched by a corresponding verification mechanism, has created conditions in which predatory journals, conferences, and award bodies can thrive. Rising demand for indexed journal publications has already produced unsolicited offers to acquire legitimate, non-profit university journals, commercializing a system meant to signal quality. The threat extends beyond obviously fraudulent venues: recent evidence of paper mines (Barnett & Byrne, 2026), in which openly available datasets are mass-mined into formulaic, artificial-intelligence-assisted manuscripts that pass peer review in ostensibly legitimate journals, shows that volume-based incentives corrupt the research record even when every formal quality marker is present. Reading the Philippine case alongside this global pattern suggests that whitelisting indexed venues is necessary but insufficient. Accountability requires Philippine authorities to complement indexing criteria with a national research integrity framework, institutional verification of authorship, conference, and data provenance, and financial support that does not make ethical publishing contingent on personal wealth.

title: Unequal Geographic Coverage of Air-Quality Monitoring across Wealth Groups in Delhi
abstract: Air-quality monitoring networks are the basis for measuring and reporting urban pollution, but their value depends in part on how well they represent the populations they are intended to serve. The study examines whether Delhi's air-quality monitoring network provides equal geographic coverage across wealth groups. It combines the locations of current air-quality monitoring stations with the Relative Wealth Index (RWI), which provides estimates of relative wealth for small geographic areas. Delhi's population is divided into five population-weighted wealth groups, and the distance from each location to the nearest monitor is calculated. Residents in the poorest wealth quintile live, on average, 7.58 km from the nearest monitor, compared with 4.69 km for the richest quintile. The difference of 2.89 km is positive even after accounting for spatial clustering (95% spatial-block bootstrap interval: 1.60 to 4.28 km). Monitoring coverage is also higher among the highest-wealth residents: 45.7% of the poorest quintile lives within 5 km of a monitor compared with 67.3% of the richest quintile. The results show that Delhi's monitoring network provides unequal geographic coverage across wealth groups. The study contributes theoretically by framing monitoring-network representativeness as an equity question. Practically, it contributes by suggesting that future network expansion consider population-weighted accessibility and coverage of lower-wealth populations along with conventional technical siting criteria. The results do not, however, show that monitors were deliberately placed to favor wealthier areas, nor do they establish that greater distance necessarily causes less accurate pollution measurement.

title: A Step, Not a Slope: The Global Rise of Anti-Government Protest, 1990–2025
abstract: Analysts have described the 2010s as an era of mass protest and expect protests to continue to increase. How did the frequency of antigovernmental protests change globally from 1990 to 2019? And what does the pattern imply for the years ahead? This is the question of the study. We used linear regression with annual counts of protests from the Mass Mobilization dataset (15,143 protests in 168 countries, 147–160 in any one year). The data was well fit by a simple linear trend (adding around 12 protests a year), but the fit was much better with a model that included a one-time shift in 2011: protests jumped by around 244 events per year after 2011, with little or no year-on-year trend. The break in 2011 was detected independently by a structural break test. After controlling for world population growth, the step remained significant. ACLED data for the period 2021-2025 did not show a significant further increase in the global total, although protests rose sharply in some countries and fell in others. Armed rebellion was not counted, so falling protest numbers may partly reflect a change in the form of dissent rather than a decline in dissent itself, as in Myanmar after 2021, where dissent became armed resistance. So global protest seems to have reached a new, higher plateau rather than to be on a steady upward climb, warning against linear projections of ever-increasing dissent.

title: Unmade Ground: Displacement, Dispossession, and the Erosion of Spatial Memory Among Kurdish Forced Migrants
abstract: Forced displacement does not merely relocate people; it dismantles the material infrastructure through which place becomes memory. Drawing on 80 semi-structured interviews with Kurdish participants in their region of origin (n=25), Central Anatolia (n=25) and Western Europe (n=30), this article examines how the destruction, abandonment and transformation of inhabited space unmakes collective and intergenerational memory. Using Cernea's (1997) Impoverishment Risks and Reconstruction model alongside Malkki's (1992) critique of sedentarist assumptions about place, the analysis identifies four interlinked processes: urban redevelopment, rural demographic hollowing, diaspora gentrification, and the institutional foreclosure of access to common and sacred land. Participants describe memory as materially anchored, carried in streets, soil and threshold spaces, so that narrative transmission alone cannot repair its loss. The article argues that spatial memory loss is a distinct impoverishment risk inadequately addressed by existing frameworks, extends Cernea's model by specifying the memorial stakes of lost access to common property, and proposes the concept of inherited spatial memory: attachment to places the second generation has never physically inhabited.

title: Cooperation as Routing: A Network-Layer Formalization of How Help Propagates Through Social Networks
abstract: Most models of how things spread on social networks are broadcast models: a state reaches whoever is reachable, and the analysis asks how far it spread. Cooperation often does not spread this way. A request for help has no xed recipient; a person who receives it either helps or, unable to help, passes it toward someone who can. Repeated, this for- warding carries the request across the network hop by hop, much as a packet is routed toward a host it has never met. Classical work on decentralized search established that such address-free messages can reach a target through local decisions, and that chains die mainly because intermediaries stop. We formalize the decision layer of this process: help- requests are packets, participants are nodes, and each node facing a request acknowledges it, forwards it, does both, or drops it. We dene an eective forward as one whose next hop itself acts, and show that crediting only eective forwards, to the immediate previous hop only, rewards every intermediary on a successful path without backward propagation, rewards routing quality rather than volume, and gives no reward for acting in isolation. We specify the provenance records needed to measure these quantities and illustrate, on the log of an operating mutual-aid platform, how chains that reached four hops could not be reconstructed because provenance was missing at the second hop. We discuss implications for cooperative multi-agent systems and for instrumenting platforms that route help.

title: Perceived Manipulation, Fairness, and Trust in Competitive Mobile Gaming: A Cross-Cultural Analysis of Player Discourse
abstract: Perceptions of fairness play a central role in player experience within competitive mobile games, yet the processes through which players develop and sustain beliefs about manipulation remain insufficiently understood. This study investigates fairness-related discourse across two cultural and platform contexts through a five-year longitudinal qualitative analysis (2022–2026) of player-generated content from competitive mobile backgammon games. The primary corpus consists of more than 52,000 Persian-language player reviews collected from Iranian app distribution platforms, supplemented by anonymised customer support transcripts. The comparative corpus comprises a stratified random sample of 750 negative reviews drawn from 4,116 reviews posted on an anglophone app-store listing over the same period. Using Inductive Thematic Analysis (ITA), the study identified seven recurring themes: dice manipulation, pay-to-win mechanics, bot opponents, connectivity sabotage, predetermined outcomes, statistical anomaly reporting, and support dismissal. These themes were subsequently organised into three higher-order meta-themes: Perceived Agency Erosion, Trust Erosion, and Statistical Misinterpretation. The findings reveal both convergent and culturally distinct patterns. Beliefs that game outcomes are manipulated through unfair dice behaviour emerged as the dominant theme in both datasets, suggesting common cognitive mechanisms underlying fairness perceptions in stochastic competitive environments. At the same time, the two contexts differed in their developmental trajectories, complaint framing, and institutional response structures. Fairness-related complaints increased substantially across the Persian-language corpus over the study period, whereas comparable concerns remained relatively stable within the anglophone sample. Players in both contexts employed statistical reasoning to support manipulation claims, although the rhetorical and cultural framing of these arguments differed. Institutional responses to complaints also varied structurally, yet both contexts exhibited patterns that players frequently interpreted as dismissive or insufficiently responsive. These findings contribute to research on player psychology, digital trust, and cross-cultural user experience by demonstrating how perceptions of unfairness emerge through the interaction of cognitive biases, community discourse, and platform communication practices. The study further highlights the importance of transparency design and context-sensitive trust-building mechanisms in competitive free-to-play games.

title: Utility Function and Labor Supply -- The case of ces functions: an elementary approach
abstract: In this note, we revisit the consumption-leisure (or equivalently, consumption-labor) trade-off and show that models relying on a Cobb-Douglas utility function (characterized by a unit substitution elasticity between leisure and consumption) obscure important elements of labor supply behavior. To this end, we explore the possibilities offered by the family of CES functions to represent the preferences of the consumer-worker agent. This choice enables us to generate a variety of labor supply functions, not necessarily monotonically increasing with respect to the real wage. Throughout the note, we explicitly highlight the dependence of the reservation wage on the substitution elasticity as well as a threshold of non-wage income crucial for its evolution. We find ourselves back in a debate that remains relevant questioning a possible disincentive effect of unemployment benefits. We begin by reviewing the definitions of key concepts and analytical tools, and the examples provided are constructed to allow for clear graphical representations.

title: Are Women Comedians Less Funny?: Empirical Analysis of Gender Differences in 1-on-1 Competitive Comedy
abstract: "Is there a difference in funniness between men and women?'" This study addresses this question. The perception that "women are less funny than men" is widespread, and some studies have indeed shown that men have a better sense of humor. In addition, in industries dominated by men, the presence of women tends to be relatively low. In the comedy industry, where men make up the overwhelming majority, women comedians are thus exposed to a double stereotype of this kind. We examined whether, under such a double stereotype, women comedians are able to be as funny as men comedians. We collected and analyzed data on a total of 3,925 matchups from a television program in which comedians compete directly over funniness in one-on-one contests. The results showed that, although a simple statistical model makes men comedians appear funnier, an analysis using a model that accounts for individual funniness revealed no significant difference in funniness between men and women. Although concerns remain about the generalizability of the findings, the results call into question existing research on gender differences in sense of humor, as well as the associated stereotypes.

title: The EU’s Biotech Industrial Policy: Between Competitiveness and Geoeconomics
abstract: This contribution examines the European Union’s emerging biotechnology industrial policy in the context of intensifying US–China technological rivalry, focusing on the relationship between competitiveness, strategic autonomy, and corporate power. The proposed EU Biotech Act seeks to strengthen the sector through regulatory simplification, public financing, strategic projects, and enhanced intellectual property protection. However, its competitiveness-oriented approach obscures the geopolitical and distributional implications of biotechnology policy. The EU’s reluctance to localise production or restrict global interdependencies is driven by the integration of European pharmaceutical multinationals into global value chains and their dependence on US markets and Chinese biotechnology ecosystem. Consequently, strategic autonomy tends to be framed as synonymous with the global profitability of pharmaceutical corporations rather than broader societal resilience. By situating the Biotech Act within debates on intellectual monopoly capitalism, this short reflection questions whether extending intellectual property rights and reducing regulatory barriers will reinforce an increasingly extractive pharmaceutical business model. It ultimately calls for reconsidering the social purpose of EU industrial policy and whether biotechnology sovereignty should prioritise corporate competitiveness or pharmaceuticals as a public good.

title: Who Does Prevention Reach? Psychosocial Risk Assessment under Brazil’s Regulatory Standard 1 (NR-1)
abstract: Employers who assess psychosocial hazards can report an improved workplace average while some workers become more exposed. Brazil's Regulatory Standard 1 has required employers to manage work-related psychosocial risk factors since May 2026, and employers are now producing their first inventories. The standard already requires them to identify exposed groups, involve workers, and monitor preventive measures. International guidance supports subgroup analysis but says less about how to verify whom a preventive measure reached. Drawing on regulatory documents and research on organizational inequality and workplace interventions, this policy analysis proposes a record that links exposure evidence to the working condition an employer decides to change, the workers each measure reaches, and the distribution of subsequent change. The record also addresses uncertainty, measurement comparability, confidentiality, and workforce turnover. Regulators and employers in countries that mandate psychosocial risk assessment can judge prevention by the overall reduction in exposure and by its distribution.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) for Coding Open-Ended Survey Responses: A Total Survey Error Framework
abstract: Open-ended questions are commonly used in survey research to supplement closed-ended questions by capturing respondents’ views, reasons, and priorities in their own words. However, coding these responses for analysis remains time-consuming and difficult to standardise. Recent advances in automated coding, especially through large language models (LLMs), have renewed interest in using open-ended responses at scale, but their evaluation is often difficult and framed mainly in terms of classification accuracy and agreement with human coding. This paper develops a Total Survey Error framework for evaluating automated coding of open-ended survey responses as part of survey measurement and data production. Model outputs are assessed using existing human-coded data as a high-quality operational benchmark, with the evaluation examining six complementary dimensions, such as processing agreement, measurement validity, prevalence distortion, coding density, response-form sensitivity, and operational reliability. The framework is applied to data using open-ended survey responses from the National Centre for Social Research (NatCen). The paper aims to inform how automated coding systems, including LLMs, can be assessed in practice, and what issues survey researchers should consider when evaluating their suitability for open-ended survey coding, and how improved coding may enable wider use of open-ended questions in large-scale quantitative surveys. Keywords: automated coding; large language models; measurement validity; open-ended survey responses; survey data quality; Total Survey Error

title: The Subnational Fertility Transition in Italy (1871-1971): A Century of Fundamental Change
authors: Riccardo Omenti, Nicola Barban, Michail Raftakis
abstract: The Italian fertility transition has drawn sustained interest from historical demographers, thanks to rich archival sources, especially parish records, and a well-established scholarly tradition. Yet no study has offered a comprehensive account of how the transition unfolded subnationally across the second half of the nineteenth and first half of the twentieth centuries. Drawing on extensive yet underutilised data from the Italian National Institute of Statistics (ISTAT), we present annual total fertility rate (TFR) estimates for all Italian provinces covering the historical period 1871–1971, using an established Bayesian modelling framework. Combining convergence analysis with measures of relative dispersion and variability, we examine whether provincial fertility differences widened or narrowed over the transition. We further investigate urban-rural fertility trajectories within Italy’s nine most populous provinces. The results reveal a geographically uneven transition: northern and central provinces led the fertility decline, while southern provinces lagged behind, resulting in divergence across provinces. Nonetheless, urban–rural differences narrowed substantially in northern and central provinces and remained negligible in southern provinces. These findings underscore the spatial heterogeneity of Italy’s fertility transition, displaying the co-existence of increasing provincial disparities with diminishing urban-rural differences in the areas leading the fertility decline.

title: Passive Behavioral Tracing: A Non-Interventional Fairness Protocol for Cooperative AI
abstract: Emerging AI governance regimes, including the EU AI Act's post-market monitoring obligation and the NIST AI RMF's measure function, require ongoing fairness monitoring but leave open which statistics should satisfy it. Interventional audits (A/B tests, counterfactual procedures, adversarial probing) manipulate the system, and often the people, under audit, and are episodic where monitoring is continuous. This article argues that a useful part of that monitoring can be done passively, and proposes Passive Behavioral Tracing (PBT), a protocol that audits fairness in AI-mediated cooperative systems using only behavioral traces the system already records. PBT formalizes four constructs computable from ordinary logs (consistency of treatment, parity across naturally occurring groups, proportionality to contribution, and drift over time) and combines them into two indicators, PBT-Ethics and PBT-Coop. A Monte Carlo study with released code shows that the constructs form two families: reciprocity and parity register unfair treatment whether it has always existed or began recently, while consistency and drift respond to change, and only drift locates when the change happened. This distinction carries regulatory weight: unfairness present since deployment implicates a system's design, while unfairness with an onset points to a dateable change, and the two call for remedies that a single score cannot separate. The study also shows the protocol's limits: mild, sustained unfairness against a small group is often missed. All results come from a stylized synthetic model; PBT is a specification validated in principle and complementary to interventional audits, not a finding about any operating system.

title: An Empirical Study on How Private College Counseling Perpetuates Structural Disadvantage A Mixed-Methods Study Combining Survey, Interview, and Social Media Content Analysis
abstract: Abstract Equitable access to higher education is widely regarded as a cornerstone of social mobility, yet the rapid growth of an independent educational consulting (IEC) industry has introduced a market-driven layer of college admissions guidance available only to families who can pay for it. This study investigates whether private college counseling functions as a neutral support service or as a mechanism of structural disadvantage that converts economic capital into institutional advantage, drawing on Pierre Bourdieu's theory of cultural and social capital. Using a triangulated, mixed-methods design, the study combines a 20-respondent Likert-scale survey of students and parents, semi-structured interviews with six purposively sampled respondent groups (student and parent users and non-users, school-based counselors, and private consultants), and an original content analysis of eight social media acceptance posts from a private counseling agency, coded against a seven-theme promotional codebook. Findings converge across all three methods: 82% of survey respondents reported that private counselors reveal "unspoken" admissions criteria unavailable to public-school peers; 65% identified fee-based, unadvertised opportunity-brokering as a distinguishing service; and interviews revealed overwhelming cross-group consensus — among both users and non-users of private counseling — that the practice constitutes an unfair structural advantage rather than a neutral commercial service. The content analysis found that aspirational imagery and institutional-legitimacy signaling appeared in 100% of coded posts, empirically confirming the marketing mechanisms respondents described. title: Enhancing Dementia Awareness and Specialized Nurse Training in the Gulf: A Policy Roadmap for Oman, Qatar, UAE, and Saudi Arabia
authors: Sukant Khurana, Sanampreet Kaur, Mohammad Saddam Khan, Gaurav Deepak Patel, Prajwal Anand, K. Vijaya Lakshmi, Sultan Ahmad, Dr. Brooks Robinson
abstract: The countries of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) are projected to see more than a threefold increase in dementia by 2050, due to a rapidly aging population. However, health care systems across Oman, Qatar, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia are still skewed towards acute rather than chronic care. Nurses are the primary dementia caregivers, but they often are not specialists. This situation is exacerbated by non-standardized curricula, heavy reliance on expatriate workforce, linguistic and cultural barriers, high workforce turnover, limited career incentives, and low public and institutional awareness, which delays diagnoses.This study synthesizes available regional and international evidence on dementia related nurse training and workforce preparedness in the GCC and develops evidence-informed policy recommendations for strengthening dementia education and workforce capacity. We propose several regional recommendations including accredited certification, compulsory continuing professional development, multidisciplinary care teams, and awareness-raising initiatives. Coordinated investment in specialized nurse training and workforce policy is important to prepare GCC healthcare systems for the region’s growing dementia burden.

title: Urban Human-Canine Conflict Mitigation: A 2023 Pilot Study on Stray Dog Population Management in Chembur, Mumbai
abstract: This study investigates the urban stray dog population in Mumbai, Maharashtra, and proposes actionable policy recommendations to mitigate human-canine conflicts. A mixed-methods retrospective pilot study was utilised, incorporating a March 2023 community survey (n=91) in the Chembur area, alongside site visits to local Non-Governmental Organisations and semi-structured interviews with Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) officials. The survey revealed that 61.53% of respondents supported the relocation of stray dogs, whereas only 21.97% supported neutering. The findings indicate a pressing need for enhanced infrastructural capacity within the Animal Birth Control (ABC) programme. Core policy recommendations include the systematic expansion of sterilisation drives, the integration of private veterinary practitioners into mass vaccination campaigns, and the strict enforcement of the Animal Birth Control Rules, 2023.

title: The Grumpy Meme and Irritability Ecology: How Low-Intensity Negative Affect Spreads, Survives, Sediments, and Becomes a Workplace Climate
abstract: Research on negative affect in organizations has largely focused on relatively visible phenomena such as anger, aggression, abusive supervision, workplace bullying, and incivility. Yet much of everyday organizational life unfolds between overt anger episodes, when no one is shouting but employees still monitor facial expressions, short replies, sighs, silence, or reduced responsiveness and conclude that someone appears grumpy. Such low-intensity signals may alter whether people approach, speak, seek advice, or share information. To theorize this domain, this paper distinguishes Irritability, Grumpiness, and the Grumpy Meme, and introduces Irritability Ecology as an integrative framework. Irritability refers to a relatively low-intensity internal affective state that need not be externally expressed. Grumpiness refers to socially perceivable expressions through which others infer that a person appears to be in a bad mood. The Grumpy Meme refers to a socio-affective transmission process in which perceived grumpiness alters another person’s affect or behavior and is subsequently re-expressed in another interaction. Thus, irritability may exist without observable grumpiness, while perceived grumpiness does not necessarily demonstrate underlying irritability. The paper argues that low-intensity negative affect may survive in workplaces because it is inexpensive to express, highly repeatable, difficult to sanction, and often protected by ambiguity regarding both the event and the actor’s intention. Repeated expressions may accumulate through Affective Sedimentation, creating background vigilance, mood-reading, and eventually a workplace climate. A two-axis model of anger and irritability is proposed, yielding four affective climate types: Calm–Stable, Quiet Tension, Eruption–Recovery, and Pervasive Anger–Irritability. The paper further introduces Affective Non-Transmission as the capacity to experience negative affect without automatically transferring it to others, and connects this capacity to post-conflict relational repair. Irritability Ecology is therefore not a weaker version of Anger Ecology. Whereas Anger Ecology examines the visible fire of workplace affect, Irritability Ecology examines the ambient climate that persists between fires. The framework shifts attention from identifying “grumpy people” to examining how low-intensity negative affect is expressed, transmitted, sustained, sedimented, interrupted, and repaired within organizational environments.

title: When Execution Is Cheap: Specification, Evaluation, and Rent Capture in AI-Enabled Work
abstract: As artificial intelligence lowers the cost of executing well-specified tasks, economic value may shift toward defining desired outcomes and evaluating machine-generated outputs. This paper examines the conditions under which that shift creates economic rents and identifies who may capture them. It separates defining success into four activities: eliciting intent, selecting among admissible specifications, ratifying a choice, and validating outputs. Two models clarify the underlying mechanisms. The first shows that gains from cheaper execution approach a ceiling determined by evaluation cost, which makes evaluator attention more consequential as generation becomes inexpensive. The second shows that generating more candidates increases the marginal value of proxy fidelity, linking abundant output to specification overfitting and Goodhart-type failures. These mechanisms indicate where value may concentrate without determining who receives the returns. Rent requires inelastic supply, exclusion from the created surplus, and the absence of cheaper substitutes. These conditions are most likely when specifications scale across many executions, ratification carries liability, trust institutions certify judgment, organizational systems control codified knowledge, or concentrated model providers set influential defaults. The analysis further distinguishes machine-checkable evaluation against a stated specification from a principal’s assessment of fit to purpose. The former is increasingly commoditized; the latter remains tied to authority, attention, and accountability. The paper develops six testable predictions and a factorial experiment examining evaluation costs, specification fidelity, authority drift, and psychological ownership. Cheap execution relocates bottlenecks, while institutions and market structure determine whether specification, evaluation, default setting, or scarce execution inputs generate rents and who captures them.

title: The prestige precedes the prize: Top-journal papers and new federal grants
abstract: Evaluators and scientists treat a top-journal paper as a step toward the next grant. We asked whether it is one. We linked 2.19 million last-authored papers by 1.07 million US scientists, 2014–2021, to new lead-investigator awards from the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation, defining top journals as the 5% most cited in their topic and year. The design rests on timing and on holding the scientist fixed: if a top-journal paper brings grants, the advantage should open after the paper. Top-journal papers were followed by a new award twice as often as other papers (55.3 against 26.3 per 1,000), yet the difference was as large two years before publication. For the same scientist, award rates after a top-journal paper and another paper differed by −0.3 per 1,000 (95% confidence interval −8.0 to 7.4), an upper limit at 25% of the difference between scientists. Researchers' small lead over matched researchers was similar before and after their first top-journal paper (3.1 and 3.3 per 1,000). Within three years, journal prestige worked mainly as a record of accumulated advantage, and the funding gap should not be read as the return on one more top-journal paper.

title: The Intersection of Fascia, Fascism, and Language: Reframing Neurodivergence as an Adaptive Response to Environmental Stress
abstract: This theoretical paper argues that global autism prevalence data are better read as a map of social ecology than as a map of biology. Diagnostic prevalence reflects the interaction of neurodevelopmental variation, distress, recognition and diagnostic access, and I argue that identified rates rise where relational buffering weakens, institutional demands intensify, and diagnostic systems are primed to read difference as dysfunction. The argument integrates three domains that are rarely analyzed together. First, fascia is treated as a body-wide communication network that densifies under chronic stress, and I propose, as a hypothesis, that the cell danger response (Naviaux, 2014, 2025) may link sustained social threat to physiological rigidity. Second, language is treated as regulatory infrastructure: drawing on Jackson et al. (2019) and Fricker’s (2007) concept of hermeneutical injustice, a dominant diagnostic language shapes how bodily states are interpreted, governed, and pathologized. Third, fascism, which shares its etymological root with fascia in the Roman fasces, is used as a conceptual analogy for systems in which control replaces communication and feedback is suppressed. Apparent anomalies in prevalence across India, Spain, Japan, Australia, and the Nordic countries are examined, and a testable prediction is stated for each. The paper distinguishes established findings from its own hypotheses throughout. The paper concludes that the aim is less distress, not less autism, which shifts intervention upstream toward environments that restore co-regulation and tolerate difference.

title: GLCI (Global Linguistic Connectivity Index): How Connected Is the World?
abstract: Eight billion people speak more than seven thousand languages. If two of them meet by chance, how likely is it that the one listening understands the one speaking, without a translator? We estimate about one chance in nine. Greenberg (1956) defined this probability for a single population as an index of communication; we compute it for the world. The data come from an audit of individual language repertoire compiled from hundreds of census, survey and reference sources, mapped onto a common conversational threshold (level A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages, CEFR) and a common individuation standard (ISO 639-3, the language codes of the International Organization for Standardization). That audit, reported with ALPS (Average Language a Person Speaks) in Hovhannisyan (2026a), covers 237 jurisdictions and 8.16 billion residents; connectivity is computed for the 216 with language-level data, which hold 8.09 billion, while the other 21, with 69 million residents, have a national ALPS value but no language rows. The audit is extended with a directional table of intelligibility between related languages, which covers 591 language pairs, most of them assessed and few measured. The resulting index, the Global Linguistic Connectivity Index (GLCI), is the probability that a randomly drawn listener comprehends a randomly drawn speaker. GLCI is 0.1129 (95% interval 0.1083–0.1176); the interval covers only row-level, sampling-type uncertainty in the input shares, and single modelling choices move GLCI between 0.096 and 0.134 (§6.1). Within a single jurisdiction the probability is 0.6284 (0.5907–0.6660), a pair-weighted figure dominated by India and China; across two jurisdictions it is 0.0747 (0.0711–0.0788), and because 91% of pairs span two jurisdictions, the lower value governs. Connectivity is concentrated: nearly a third of cross-jurisdiction pair mass lies below 0.01, and the median pair sits at 0.022. It also rests on one language. English carries 39.2% of global connectivity and 61.9% of the connectivity between countries. In a simple model relating repertoire to connectivity, which languages are learned matters far more than how many. At a mean repertoire of four languages per person, GLCI is 98%, 58% or 15% depending on the allocation rule, that is, chiefly on which languages are learned and also on where. Compared with a dataset that other researchers built from Ethnologue, the LINGACON estimates agree closely on first languages (r = 0.951). On the full layer, leaving out the intelligibility term that the other dataset lacks, they are 1.45 times higher, and the difference lies mainly in the coverage of acquired languages.

title: The ALPS Index: A Global Estimate of the Average Number of Languages a Person Speaks
abstract: How many languages does the average person speak? The question has an established qualitative answer, that "probably more than half of the world's population is bilingual" (Grosjean, 2012), but no quantitative one at global scale. We audited individual language repertoire in 237 jurisdictions with 8.16 billion residents. Survey, census and reference sources were mapped onto a common conversational threshold (CEFR level A2) and a common individuation standard (ISO 639-3), graded on a seven-band evidentiary scale, and treated for twelve documented biases of census and survey instruments. The resulting index, ALPS (Average Language a Person Speaks), is the population mean of individual repertoire size. The global population-weighted value is 1.568 languages per person. Its grade band, 1.42 to 1.70, reflects the evidentiary grade of the sources, not sampling error. The alternative specifications we could compute place the figure between 1.53 and 1.60; an adjustment for the ages of survey respondents lowers it by at least 0.041; the value documented by official and survey instruments alone is 1.48. As a mean, the figure limits the share of people who speak two or more languages to no more than 57% (42%–70% across the band). The unweighted mean across jurisdictions (1.87) is well above the weighted mean: individual multilingualism is concentrated in smaller populations. Group-level linguistic diversity and individual repertoire are only moderately associated (r = 0.43). A direct arithmetic test locates incomplete domestic bridging: in ten jurisdictions holding 38.9% of the audited population, mean repertoire is below the level that complete bridging through the largest first language would require; in three of them (India, Ethiopia and Côte d'Ivoire, 19.8%) the shortfall exceeds the jurisdiction's band. The audit synthesises existing sources and involves no new fieldwork. Its central limitation is that source quality is distributed inversely to linguistic diversity. For each specification choice whose effect can be computed, we report the value the alternative would produce; the choices whose effect cannot be computed are named.

title: Exploring Nonlinear Associations Between AI Comment Volume and Retail Investor Sentiment
abstract: Artificial intelligence comment generators have proliferated in online stock forums. However, how AI comment volume associates with retail investor sentiment, and whether this association is conditional on market volatility and annual AI comment density, remain under-explored. Using weekly data from the East Money Stock Forum and the Shanghai Composite Index spanning May 2019–October 2024 in China, this paper proposed a two-detector ensemble for AI comment detection, then investigated nonlinear associations between AI comment volume and retail investor sentiment under three tiers of market volatility and six annual AI comment densities. Our generalized additive model (GAM) results show that AI comment volume exhibits a weak, net-positive nonlinear association with mean retail investor sentiment, and a very weak net-negative nonlinear association with sentiment divergence. We find no statistically significant pairwise differences in these associations across low-, medium- and high-volatility levels. For annual AI comment density, statistically significant cross-density differences are observed for sentiment standard deviation in multiple year pairwise comparisons, whereas only one comparison yields significant differences for mean sentiment. Collectively, our findings indicate that merely considering the number of AI comments provides limited information regarding the sentiment of retail investors.

title: The geopolitics of academic publishing: the case of Kazakhstan
abstract: Abstract Publications in Scopus- and Web of Science-indexed journals have become the global benchmark of academic excellence. This article examines how Kazakhstan has placed this new ‘gold standard’ at the centre of its academic publishing policy, which has become a key part of its university reform agenda since 2010. Using a Gramscian lens on power and knowledge, we show how the government employs this policy to position itself between the West and Russia in a shifting geopolitical context. The adoption of this benchmark not only changes how Kazakhstan's academic community relates to the broader academic world. It also significantly reshapes the hierarchy within Kazakhstan’s academic community. We argue that this has profound implications for the societal role of universities and academic research and their ability to address local challenges. Our study makes both empirical and theoretical contributions to the growing literature on the geopolitics of knowledge, highlighting the interplay among local, national, and global dynamics.

title: Who protects Science Diplomacy from being weaponised? The role of domestic policies
abstract: Many researchers have voiced concerns about the weaponisation of policy-relevant international research collaborations. But why does this pose a problem? This contribution develops a Neo-Gramscian notion of science diplomacy to explain how processes of weaponisation risk undermining the mediation role of scientific research, its capacity to integrate diverse perspectives and values, and, consequently, its ability to mediate between conflicting norms, values and interests. Drawing on Nicos Poulantzas’s state theory, the article further elaborates the concept of mediation and illuminates the role of national parliaments as an important mediator between academia and civil society, more generally, and the government. The empirical study explores parliamentary deliberations of the UK National Security Bill in the House of Commons and the House of Lords. It shows how the parliamentary scrutiny failed to curb the significant expansion of governmental authority justified in the name of security, with important consequences for how academics engage with other governments as part of science diplomacy. The findings shed light on the significance of public policy and domestic political struggles for international politics. In the context of an ongoing crisis of multilateralism, domestic political dynamics have become even more important.

title: Climate Change and the Socio-Political Foundations of Welfare
