abstract: As climate change and decarbonization become central sources of political conflict in Europe, welfare states are increasingly invoked as institutions capable of cushioning transition costs, managing distributional conflict, and stabilizing democratic legitimacy. The article identifies three perspectives in which this expectation appears: green-growth approaches expect welfare institutions to secure the social conditions of low-carbon accumulation; social-democratic and labour-oriented approaches seek to renew class compromise through just transition policies; and post-growth or sustainable-welfare approaches ask whether welfare can be reorganized around needs, sufficiency, and planetary boundaries. Despite their differences, all three perspectives rely on a shared assumption: that the welfare state can provide socio-political stability under ecological constraint. This article problematizes this assumption by reconstructing the historical foundations of welfare-state stabilization. It argues that twentieth-century welfare capitalism functioned as a form of socio-political glue: it mediated the tension between capitalist market inequalities and democratic claims to equality by making market dependence bearable, class compromise plausible, and bounded solidarity legitimate. Yet this glue was fossil in character. It depended on sustained growth, fossil-energy regimes with underpriced social and ecological costs, institutionalized labour relations, nationally bounded solidarity, and the externalization of social and ecological costs. Climate change unsettles each of these stabilizing mechanisms. It strains the growth-dependent balance between commodification and decommodification; reconfigures class compromise by politicizing fossil-dependent forms of production, consumption, status, and deservingness; and destabilizes closure and containment by making externalized costs return materially, politically, and morally. The article therefore argues that climate change should not be understood only as a new generation of social risks to be absorbed by existing welfare institutions. More fundamentally, it challenges the welfare state’s historically established capacity to process risks, conflicts, and legitimacy claims in familiar ways. Rather than presuming which form of “green glue” should replace the fossil compromise, it calls for a more systematic analysis of the democratic conflicts through which competing projects of welfare-state stabilization are negotiated: who should be protected, who should pay, which losses count as legitimate, which ways of life remain publicly recognized, and through which democratic procedures new forms of socio-political glue can be built under ecological constraint.

title: Why the Left Leans Socialist and the Right Leans Capitalist: Class, Coalitions and Where the Link Breaks
abstract: Political labels are often assumed to map neatly onto economic systems: the left is expected to favor socialism and the right capitalism. This paper asks why that pattern exists and why it breaks down in some countries. It first examines four explanations for the pattern: historical origins, class interest, core values, and coalition bundling. It then compares cases, including Sweden, China, the United States and India, where party labels and economic policy diverge. The paper argues that the link between political stance and economic policy is contingent rather than necessary, and that it varies with a party's voter base, a country's history, and its state capacity. The findings suggest that left-right labels are an unreliable guide to actual economic policy.

title: Does Crop Diversification Improve Rural Household Income in Bangladesh?
abstract: This paper examines whether crop diversification improves household income among rural farming households in Bangladesh, using data from the Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES) 2022. Using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression with division fixed effects and robust standard errors, the study finds that diversification has a strong and stable positive effect on crop sales income, but not on total household income once household characteristics are controlled. This suggests that diversification operates primarily through the agricultural income channel. The findings carry practical implications for agricultural extension policy in Bangladesh.

title: Who Manufactured Pseudo-History Theories? The Emergent Collective Creation of Historical Narratives on the Chinese Internet
abstract: This paper examines the formation, expansion, and functions of pseudo-history theories (伪史论) on the Chinese internet from the perspective of cultural economics, and proposes the analytical concept of “Emergent Collective Creation.” This concept refers to the process whereby a large number of relatively independent content producers, acting on the basis of their respective local motivations and in the absence of any unified overall plan, generate a collective narrative system that exceeds the original planning and control of any single participant through imitation, competition, the recombination of arguments, and the migration of topics. The paper first investigates relevant figures who possess formal academic credentials or publishing experience and analyzes the pathways through which early pseudo-history resources entered public circulation. It then takes as examples the extension of pseudo-history theories from ancient Greece and Rome to other civilizations, historical figures, and issues concerning Chinese dynastic history, exploring how competition for traffic, content imitation, and the selective recombination of historical materials drive narrative expansion. Finally, using online controversies surrounding the film The Penghu Naval Battle as a case study, it analyzes how pseudo-history theories have been deployed by different participants in conflicts over historical identity and in online opinion confrontation, and discusses possible links between controversial historical discourses and public trust in academic authority. The paper argues that even dispersed individual actions lacking unified coordination may, through indirect interaction, produce collective narrative outcomes and enable pseudo-history theories to move from a form of content competition for traffic into ideological contention. Because this study relies primarily on publicly available online materials, publications, and media reports, and lacks internal platform data as well as continuous records at the creator level, the mechanisms identified remain exploratory explanations whose chains of transmission, causal relations, and actual effects await further verification.

title: Agreement under abstention: an agreement–abstention–conflict triple and sharp bounds for Fleiss' kappa
authors: Maikel Yelandi Leyva Vázquez, Alexis Matheu Pérez, Bastián Gutiérrez Vargas
abstract: Raters in agreement studies are often allowed to abstain, for example by answering "can't tell" or "unsure". Abstentions are usually deleted or recoded, and each treatment carries an untested assumption about why raters abstained. We show how to report Fleiss' kappa without such an assumption. Assigning the abstentions to categories changes both the observed agreement and the category totals that determine chance agreement, so the extremes of kappa require optimising the two jointly. A dynamic programme gives the exact extremes over all such completions for two or three categories, with completions that attain and thereby certify them; closed-form bounds enclose them for more categories. A budget interval and tipping points grade conclusions by how far the missing ratings must depart from a reference predictive model. The shares of agreeing, abstaining and conflicting rater pairs, (pA, pU, pC), serve as an intuitive summary. Under independent sampling of units the sample extremes converge to the population identified set, and an exploratory unit bootstrap supports a three-outcome decision: adequate, inadequate or undetermined. In simulations at 2–10% abstention, estimator errors depended on the mechanism; the budget interval contained the complete-data kappa in 97–100% of replicates under random abstention but 44–51% under value-dependent abstention, and population decisions were undetermined in 43–76% of replicates. In crowdsourced weather-sentiment labels, listwise deletion declared agreement adequate where the three-outcome decision was undetermined; in safety ratings of chatbot conversations, listwise estimates fell on both sides of the interval.

title: Domestic and Family Violence Training Programs for Primary Healthcare Workforces: A Scoping Review
authors: Bibek Chauhan, Shauna Fjaagesund, Amy Homes, Katrina Andrews, Gregory Nash, Chrystie Myketiak, Kylie Roberson, Sara Richards, Florin Oprescu
abstract: Purpose Domestic and family violence (DFV) is prevalent, and primary healthcare professionals may be well placed to identify and support victim-survivors; however, limited training and organizational support can constrain safe responses. This review mapped DFV training programs for primary healthcare workforces, including targeted groups, content, delivery, and evaluation. Methods A scoping review was conducted using the Joanna Briggs Institute framework and reported according to PRISMA-ScR. PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, and PsycINFO were searched for peer-reviewed studies published from 2016 to 2026. Eligible studies evaluated the characteristics, implementation, or outcomes of DFV workforce training in primary healthcare. Of 1,262 records identified, 16 studies met the inclusion criteria. Results Training most often targeted general practitioners (n = 11) and nurses or midwives (n = 9); administrative staff (n = 4) and practice managers (n = 3) were less frequently included. Common content included DFV identification and inquiry, disclosure response, referral, risk assessment, and safety planning. Face-to-face workshops predominated, often supplemented by mentoring, case discussion, role-play, and implementation support. Evaluations mainly assessed short-term knowledge, confidence, and preparedness; sustained practice and organizational outcomes were assessed less often. Conclusions DFV training may improve primary healthcare professionals’ knowledge, confidence, and preparedness to support victim-survivors, but predominantly short-term and self-reported outcomes limit conclusions about sustained clinical change. Evidence gaps remain in organizational readiness, workforce agency, long-term implementation, and inclusion of non-clinical staff.

title: Redundancy by design: The bicycle and intermodality as pillars of transport resilience in emergencies, with lessons from Japan
abstract: Transport systems are optimised for efficiency in normal conditions, yet their performance in emergencies depends on a property that efficiency tends to erode: redundancy. This paper argues that intermodality, understood as the organised capacity to combine and substitute modes within a jour-ney, is the most practical way to build redundancy into mobility systems, and that the bicycle holds a distinctive place in this architecture because it is energy-autonomous, space-efficient, widely owned, repairable and able to use almost any route left passable after a shock. Building on a framework that links resilience, redundancy and intermodality, the paper reviews evidence from Japan, where cycling is embedded in everyday travel through social acceptance rather than dedicated policy, and where the 1995, 2011 and 2018 earthquakes exposed both the vulnerability of fuel- and grid-dependent modes and the spontaneous substitution role of the bicycle. These observations are compared with transit strikes in Paris, London and Montréal, metro closures in Washington, the COVID-19 pandemic in New York and European cities, and counter-examples in New Orleans and Fort McMurray, where the lack of modal or network redundancy left people stranded. The analysis shows that redundancy works only when it is exercised daily: a mode that is not owned, practised, socially accepted and connected to public transport in normal times cannot be mobilised in a crisis. The paper proposes three condi-tions, availability, capability and connectivity, together with phase-based planning measures, and discusses the limits of the bicycle regarding distance, density, age, weather and safety. It concludes that everyday bicycle and public transport intermodality is a low-cost insurance that planning should value explicitly.

title: Unequal Parenting across Childhood: How Class Differences in Parental Control of Screen Use Reverse with the Child's Age
abstract: Research usually treats class differences in parenting style as constant throughout childhood. We show instead that they can reverse with the child's age. Our case is parental control of children's screen use, for which expert advice is restrictive when children are young and divided when they are adolescents. We draw on an original survey of 20,670 Norwegian households with children aged 3 to 17 to estimate class differences in time limits, control of content and the negotiation of rules at each age. We find that better-resourced parents are stricter than others with young children, but more permissive with adolescents. The composition of the resources available to the household shapes the pattern: income and education have different, complementary associations with parental control. The observed reversal across childhood suggests that the advantage of well-resourced families in child rearing lies less in a fixed repertoire of practices than in adaptability, a capacity to adjust as the appropriate practice changes with the child's age.

title: The Impact of Maternal Preconception Health on Long-Term Child Health and Developmental Outcomes: A Scoping Review
authors: Catherine Stewart, Katie Harron, Jennifer Hall
abstract: The preconception period is a critical window during which maternal health and behaviours can influence pregnancy and offspring outcomes. However, preconception care remains limited, and existing research has largely focused on short-term pregnancy or neonatal outcomes. This scoping review aimed to synthesise evidence on the associations between maternal preconception health and long-term health, developmental, and educational outcomes in children. Primary studies were eligible if they examined the independent effect of maternal preconception health on child health and developmental outcomes assessed after age 1 year and up to 18 years. Five databases (MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science) were searched. Data were extracted using a standardised form and summarised descriptively. Studies were mapped by type of preconception exposure and child outcome. From 9,539 records identified, 186 studies met the inclusion criteria. Preconception BMI was the most frequently studied exposure (n=130) while neuro/cognitive development (n=83) was the most common outcome. Higher preconception BMI was consistently associated with adverse long-term outcomes, including higher offspring BMI and poorer cognitive, behavioural, and developmental outcomes. Pre-existing maternal physical and mental health conditions were also linked to poorer child health and developmental outcomes. Evidence for preconception smoking, alcohol, and substance use was limited but suggested potential harms, while diet quality and supplementation were generally associated with beneficial outcomes. These findings highlight the preconception period as a key opportunity for intervention to support positive outcomes for children and underscore the need for higher-quality, long-term research to inform policy and practice.

title: Safe (felt) by design: Understanding cyclists’ needs for traffic guidance at roadworks – A mixed-methods study on behaviour, perception, and infrastructure requirements
authors: Frederik Hilden, Peer-Benedikt Degen, Robin von Elm, Angela Francke
abstract: Introduction: Urban construction sites frequently disrupt cycling infrastructure and create safety risks for vulnerable road users. Despite regulatory frameworks for temporary traffic management, cyclists often encounter unclear or unsafe guidance around roadworks. Empirical evidence on how cyclists actually respond to such conditions remains limited. This study investigates cyclists’ behaviour, routing decisions, and safety perceptions at urban construction sites. Method: A mixed-methods design combined behavioural observations and a nationwide survey. Observational data were collected at four construction sites in Hamburg, Germany using inductive loop sensors and video recordings, capturing 146.168 bicycle passages. Behavioural interactions were coded to identify compliance, routing choices, and conflict-avoidance strategies. In addition, a web-based survey of 1,071 cyclists across Germany examined perceived safety, behavioural adaptation, and infrastructure preferences at roadworks. Results: Observational analysis identified substantial deviations from designated traffic guidance: 42% of 790 coded cyclist interactions involved non-compliant behaviour, such as riding on sidewalks or against the intended direction. Route choice was primarily influenced by motorized traffic volume and pavement quality. Cyclists frequently selected routes that maximized perceived safety and riding comfort rather than following formal guidance. Despite frequent non-compliance, cyclists often adopted cooperative strategies, including speed reduction and conflict avoidance with pedestrians. Conclusions: The findings highlight a gap between formally regulated traffic guidance and cyclists’ safety perceptions and behaviour. Temporary infrastructure that lacks clarity, comfort, or protection can lead to widespread deviations from prescribed routes. Practical applications: Temporary traffic management at construction sites should prioritize intuitive guidance, surface quality, and physical separation from motorized traffic. Incorporating cyclist needs into roadwork design can reduce conflicts and improve safety for vulnerable road users.

title: Who stops answering? Breakoff, smartphone use and educational bias in a web survey
authors: Alžbeta Ľudmová, Martin Kreidl, Barbora Hubatková, Martin Lakomý
abstract: Survey data collection has been moving towards the online self-administered mode (CAWI), which is usually seen as an effective answer to falling response rates and rising fieldwork costs. This mode, however, comes with drawbacks of its own, especially when respondents use a smartphone to fill out the survey. Related major challenge is a higher tendency of these respondents to break off, i.e. to end the interview before completion. Breakoff matters most when it occurs non-randomly and compounds existing biases, such as those based on age or education. To find out whether it does, we used questionnaire data and paradata from the CAWI component of the first wave of the second cycle of the Czech Generations and Gender Survey (2020–2022; N = 5,468, 244 breakoffs). Treating each of 118 unfiltered questionnaire items as one unit of analytical time, we analysed progression through the questionnaire using Cox regression supplemented by Kaplan–Meier survival curves. Younger respondents broke off somewhat more often than older ones, though the difference was not statistically robust. The education gradient was both steeper and more persistent: 7% of the least educated broke off as compared with 3% of the most educated, and device only partly explained this gap, leaving education and device to operate as largely independent processes. The gap was, however, concentrated on small screens - among smartphone users, breakoff rose from 4% among the most educated to over 11% among the least educated, while on larger devices it stayed flat at 3–4%. Breakoff thus adds to, rather than merely reflects, the educational bias of self-completion samples. Keywords: breakoff; web surveys; smartphone; device effects; survival analysis; paradata; representativity; Generations and Gender Survey

title: Under what conditions does complexity become unmanageable? A capacity threshold for megaprojects
abstract: Purpose. Project complexity research describes complexity in rich dimensional detail but rarely states the condition under which it stops being manageable. This paper states one and derives what remains possible past it. Design/methodology/approach. Conceptual theory elaboration from the delivering organization’s standpoint, building on requisite variety, organizational information processing and bounded rationality, illustrated with a worked calculation and a documented revision series from a public inquiry. Findings. Complexity becomes unmanageable from within at a point of no return: when the capacity demanded of a governance level exceeds the information-processing capacity available to it, set by its binding constraint, to the degree that the level can no longer remove its overload with its own means. Past it the feasible response set collapses to three moves, deceleration, external capacity and requirement reduction, because every other method consumes the missing capacity. In megaprojects the threshold falls early, because both sides of the balance are fixed before work begins. The Elbphilharmonie's public record shows the predicted signature: revisions moved both ways before contract award and one way after it. Research limitations/implications. The threshold is stated as a testable claim, not a measured constant. Five propositions with falsification conditions follow. Originality/value. Not a new inventory of complexity but a threshold within the inherited mechanism, and the identification of the translation of requirements into demanded capacity as the operation where complexity becomes subjective and manageable.

title: Overcoming inertia: Addressing barriers to managing coastal legacy waste in a changing climate
authors: Isabel Cotton, James J. Porter, James S. Robinson, Rhys H.S. Kelly, Ute Kelly, Megan Clinch, Rhys E. M. Jones, Deborah P. Dixon, Patrick Diamond, Suzy O’Hara
abstract: Climate change will increase the number of legacy waste sites (older waste sites without pollution control mechanisms) that are at risk of coastal flooding and erosion in the UK and worldwide. Whilst the need to adapt to coastal change is well documented, the combined risks of coastal change and legacy waste has received less attention. Through interviews and workshops with policy stakeholders, this paper explores current perspectives on the barriers to managing coastal legacy waste in England and Scotland. Both the interviews and workshops reveal a high awareness of the potential risks from coastal legacy waste. However, limited sources of funding, alongside knowledge gaps on the nature of pollutant risk, many competing priorities at a local authority level, and a lack of clarity on roles and responsibilities, is creating an inertia that frustrates the proactive management of the issue. Using Moser and Ekstrom’s (2010) adaptation planning cycle as an analytical framework, findings reveal that managing legacy waste is unable to progress beyond the first stage of adaptation planning due to these systemic barriers. Overall, findings indicate the urgent need for a long-term strategy designed at a national level that provides sufficient resources and capacity-building for proactive local governance.

title: Extractive conditionality: Participation and datafication in the Netherlands
abstract: Research on welfare conditionality has shown how access to social assistance is tied to behavioural and informational obligations. It has paid less attention to what recipients’ compliance produces for welfare institutions. This article develops the concept of extractive conditionality to describe arrangements in which activities and information provided under conditions of material dependency are transformed into institutionally usable resources. Drawing on an interpretive case study of Dutch social assistance, the analysis combines autobiographical testimony with policy documents, official evaluations and investigative journalism. It identifies two dimensions of extraction. First, activation requirements mobilise recipients’ time and activity even when they do not facilitate durable labour-market exit. Second, disclosure requirements generate information that can be standardised and reused for purposes such as organisational oversight and risk classification. These processes are extractive when recipients have little control over how their compelled contributions are subsequently used. The article further develops the hypothesis that this institutional productivity may help reproduce conditional arrangements despite their limited success in reducing welfare dependency. It shows how policies may fail to achieve their stated objectives while continuing to generate organisational capacities. The concept redirects analysis from what conditionality demands towards what compliance produces, who can use these outputs and how they may contribute to the persistence of conditional welfare.

title: The Digital Undertow of Penal Supervision: An Ethnography of Electronic Monitoring in Belgium
abstract: Electronic monitoring (EM) relies on digital systems to supervise people in the community, but these systems also organise the work of monitoring officers. This article examines how digital monitoring systems shape officers’ everyday work and decisions, and how these practices give meaning to penal supervision. It draws on 74 days of observation and 22 interviews with control-room officers in Belgium, conducted between 2014 and 2017. Using a strong sociomaterial perspective and the concept of the digital undertow, the analysis connects three aspects of supervision: the recording and potential scrutiny of officers’ activities, their assessments of monitored individuals, and their emphasis on rule-following. The findings show how telephone exchanges, software records and organisational expectations together shape what requires attention, and which responses count as responsible work. Officers interpret compliance as preparation for reintegration, while accurate and traceable actions become ways of demonstrating professional responsibility. These practices involve judgement and negotiation, even when officers describe their decisions as required by rules. The article contributes to research on digital penal work by showing how the practical organisation of information connects assessments of monitored individuals to standards of professional competence. It identifies processes through which institutional values acquire meaning in everyday supervision.

title: Spiritual Healing Methods in Los Angeles: the Cultural Heritage and Western Representation of Alternative Medicines
abstract: Throughout the United States of America, complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) has become increasingly popular over the past fifty years. These include any practices that stem from tradition and spirituality rather than practices that are derived from empirical evidence. With many popular spiritual healing practices originating from specific traditions across the world and across a wide range of time, there is much to explore about the mechanisms through which culturally specific spiritual healing practices adapt to Western consumerist culture. In the current study, we examine the cultural origins and development of CAM, mostly the use and popularization of Reiki, Yoga, and ayahuasca. We interviewed six spiritual health practitioners in the greater Los Angeles area to understand the modern CAM practitioner’s perspective on how spiritual healing methods have taken hold in Western culture, how they align with the original practice’s tradition, and how they have adapted to modern consumer culture. This study explores how Los Angeles’ cultural emphasis on individuality and marketability has cultivated an environment for its population to disseminate and recontextualize traditional spiritual healing methods to fit contemporary mental health demands.

title: Issue Accountability Among Public Meeting Commenters
abstract: Standard theories of accountability suggest politicians respond to voter preferences for fear of electoral sanction, yet many voters are ill-informed about policy actions. One solution to this tension is that a small group of highly engaged citizens, an issue public, may generate the conditions for accountability. We test this claim by tracking over 7,000 members of the public who submit comments on land use policies in San Francisco, CA. We measure commenters’ expressed preferences on proposed agenda items, survey them following the decision, and observe subsequent political activity with administrative data. We show that over three-quarters of commenters accurately recall their past positions, but most do not learn the subsequent policy action and rarely update their political attitudes. However, we find that a subset of anti-development voters are more likely to contribute to ideologically aligned candidates when they do not see their preferred policies enacted; yet pro-development commenters do not.

title: The economic impact of social prescribing programmes: A systematic review of 83 economic evaluations
authors: Daisy Fancourt, Holly Crudgington, Nikita Arslanovksi, Henry Aughterson, Robert J Booth, Sulia Celebi, Daniel Hayes, Jessica Sarah Kurland, Jane Morgan-Daniel, Virginia Pesata
abstract: Background Social prescribing (SP) is increasingly being adopted internationally to address non-medical, health-related social needs through referral to community-based supports and services. Although economic arguments have been central to the policy development of SP, the health economic evidence base remains fragmented. We systematically reviewed peer-reviewed and grey literature on the economic impacts of SP globally. Methods Following our PROSPERO registered record (CRD420251235365) and PRISMA and ISPOR guidance, we searched twelve bibliographic databases and 34 grey literature sources from inception to March 30, 2026. Studies of any design reporting economic outcomes or economic evaluations of SP were eligible. Risk of bias was assessed using design-specific appraisal tools. Owing to methodological heterogeneity, findings were narratively synthesised. Findings Seventy-three sources met inclusion criteria (39 peer-reviewed and 34 grey literature publications), yielding 76 studies and 83 economic analyses. Most studies were conducted in the UK (67 [88%]) and involved adults (74 [97%]). Analyses comprised 17 partial economic evaluations, 15 full economic evaluations, 47 return-on-investment evaluations, and four decision-modelling studies. Overall, 61 (77%) analyses reported economically favourable outcomes, six (8%) reported mixed findings, and 12 (15%) reported unfavourable outcomes. SP delivery costs were generally low, with annual savings ranging from £78·20-£670 per participant. Cost-per-quality-adjusted life-year estimates at 12 months ranged from £2137-£12111 and were generally below accepted willingness-to-pay thresholds. Social return on investment estimates were typically positive, ranging from £0·96-£7·08 returned per £1 invested over 12 months. Variation in estimated value was driven primarily by analytical perspective and outcomes monetised rather than intervention type, follow-up duration, or study quality. Interpretation The economic evidence base for SP is substantially larger than previously recognised but narrow healthcare-demand models underestimate its wider cross-sectoral value. Future evaluations must broaden valuation boundaries and develop financing models that reflect how costs and returns are distributed across sectors; absence of demonstrated sector-specific savings should not be interpreted as absence of value.

title: Resisting Autocratization: Pro-Democratic Protest and Leader Approval
authors: Yuko Sato, Kyosuke Kikuta, Renzo Ovidio Aurazo Diaz, Yoshikuni Ono
abstract: Civic resistance can promote democratization and counter autocratization, but when do prodemocratic protests erode support for incumbent leaders? We argue that such protests provide two informational signals: they highlight threats to democratic institutions and convey the legitimacy and collective capacity of opposition actors. Combining protest-event data with Gallup World Poll data, we leverage the as-if random timing of interviews around protest events in 64 countries between 2008 and 2020. Among more than 58,000 respondents surveyed immediately before or after these events, pro-democratic protests reduce leader approval by about 9 percentage points relative to other protests, which produce no comparable decline. The effect is stronger for sufficiently large, nonviolent protests and in autocracies, but weaker under repression. These findings show that pro-democratic protests can weaken incumbent support by making democratic threats more salient and strengthening opposition credibility, identifying a micro-level pathway through which civic resistance may counter autocratization.

title: Understanding climate actions: The cost-impact trade-off
abstract: Why do individuals commit to some climate actions but not others? Although concern about climate change is widespread, stated willingness to act often falls short. In a preregistered between-subjects survey experiment with UK respondents (N = 900), we randomly assigned participants to one of four climate actions that differ in personal cost and environmental impact: reducing meat consumption (high cost, high impact), reducing car use (high cost, moderate impact), reducing food waste (low cost, moderate impact), and reducing plastic waste (low cost, low impact). After receiving standardized information about their assigned action, participants reported their stated commitment to adopting it, their compensatory green beliefs, their expectations about others' commitment, and the share of others who would need to adopt the action before they would do so themselves (i.e., individual threshold for behavioural change).} We found that participants correctly perceived differences in the cost of the action, but misjudged environmental impact, substantially underestimating the impact of high-impact actions like dietary change and overestimating the impact of limiting plastic waste. \hl{Consistent with the reasoning behind the low-cost hypothesis}, low-cost actions elicited higher and more homogeneous \hl{stated} commitment, lower and more homogenous thresholds for \hl{behavioural change, and greater potential for social tipping}. On an individual level, we also found indications that actions that are perceived to be more costly are positively associated with compensatory green beliefs. Finally, individuals exhibited a systematic ``better-than-average'' bias, though this bias disappears among low-commitment individuals facing high-cost actions. \hl{Objective environmental impact added little once cost was taken into account, although actions that participants perceived as more impactful elicited higher commitment. In terms of policy, our results suggest that low-cost actions are a promising target for norm-based interventions, whereas high-cost, high-impact actions such as reducing meat consumption call for measures that lower their personal cost.

title: Chapter 2: Surprise, Revisited: An EU Performance Evaluation of the Arab Uprisings
abstract: Most actors and commentators across the West were caught by surprise when anti-government protests started in Tunisia and then spread across the Middle East and North Africa in the winter of 2010-2011. The events became known as the Arab Spring, the Arab revolutions or, as will be used in this volume, the ‘Arab uprisings’. This sense of surprise when the uprisings started applies to the institutions of the European Union and its major allies in the region – the United States, France and the UK, with their dense network of contacts, embassies and intelligence operatives. Nor, as will be discussed below, did any of the big NGOs or mainstream media working and reporting on the Middle East and North Africa emit clear warnings on the prospect of such an event. Even once the protests started in Tunisia in the third week of December 2010, the rapidly growing discontent in both Tunisia and Egypt initially went largely unreported in Western media as well as in reporting from the big NGOs, some of whom were at the time largely focusing on the impasse in Iraq and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. This volume, amongst others, asks to what extent and when ‘being surprised’ is to be expected, and when it indicates failures in intelligence collection, analysis, communication, or receptivity. In this chapter it will be argued that only after investigating in detail which characteristics of the Arab uprisings were particularly surprising to the European institutions and to what extent, and whether these degrees of surprise were spread evenly across analysists and decision-makers, it is possible to properly explain why the Arab uprisings were so surprising. In keeping with the aims of this volume, this subsequently serves to identify to what extent the surprising nature of the Arab uprisings, and any potential errors made in anticipating this event by the European Union, were excusable given the complexity and diagnostic difficulty of the Arab Uprisings, or whether they point to broader structural problems and shortcomings in the European intelligence-policy nexus.

title: Lessons learnt? The EU and the Arab uprisings
abstract: A reboot of the Arab Uprisings has become more likely in the wake of the COVID-19 Pandemic. In order to assess whether the European institutions are currently better able to anticipate an event such as the Arab Uprisings, this paper contends one must first investigate in depth what made the Arab Uprisings so surprising, and to whom. Hereto, this paper unpacks this surprising nature of the Uprisings and the performance of the EEAS, INTCEN and DG NEAR, challenging some of the extant explanations in this literature. To this aim and following previous research, it dissects surprise into three elements. By unpacking who was surprised (the spread of the surprise), on what (the scope of the surprise) and to what degree (the dissonance of the surprise), it complements the extant literature which prioritizes the explanation of their ‘surprisingness’ over an in-depth investigation of the characteristics which made the Arab Uprisings so surprising. It subsequently probes which factors negatively affected the EU’s performance, preparing the field for the learning of specific lessons.

title: Born to Govern or to Extract? Party types across administrative levels in Colombia
abstract: Political parties and corruption research relies predominantly on political spectrum, overlooking the organisational attributes that shape whether parties constrain or facilitate corrupt behaviour. This paper proposes a typological framework that classifies parties by their organisational origins — traditional, personalistic, ethnic, rebelorigin, and neo-Pentecostal — and examines how these are related to corruption across mayoral, gubernatorial, and presidential administrative levels. Drawing on prosecutorial records from Colombia’s Attorney General covering 2011–2020, I construct a composite corruption indicator for 1,122 municipalities across three local and two presidential elections. The empirical strategy combines municipality and two-way fixed effects, spatial econometric models, and a regression discontinuity design exploiting close elections. The results show that rebel-origin parties and citizen-signature movements consistently reduce corruption, whilst traditional and personalistic types remain statistically indistinguishable; ethnic parties appear insignificant in the main classification, but the sensitivity analysis reveals that once parapolitically captured parties are reassigned, genuine indigenous parties significantly reduce rent-seeking. This relationship varies across governmental tiers: party structure binds at the municipal level, church-based accountability operates at the gubernatorial level, and armed-group networks override party type at the presidential level. Voter turnout is positively associated with municipal corruption, consistent with clientelistic mobilisation. These findings demonstrate that how parties are built matters for understanding corruption in multi-party democracies.

title: Leaves instead of ballots: The Colombian formal and informal governance of coca
abstract: Colombia produces more coca than ever, yet scholarship remains anchored in security frameworks that overlook how institutional configurations shape this illegal crop. This article treats coca cultivation as a governance outcome, arguing that the interaction between formal institutions — political parties and electoral processes — and informal entities — criminal and rebel armed groups — determines where coca takes root. Drawing on a municipality-level panel covering the national territory from 2011 to 2023, and employing fixed effects, spatial Durbin models, and a difference-in-differences leveraging the 2016 peace settlement, the analysis reveals that no party or coalition bears a significant association with coca once municipal heterogeneity is absorbed. What persistently predicts cultivation is electoral fraud risk and armed group presence, specially the ELN guerrilla. The latest peace accord caused coca expansion rather than contraction. These findings suggest that phasing out coca demands strengthening democracy and extending the rule of law to plantation clusters.

title: How Do Unconditional Cash Transfers Break the Poverty Trap? Identifying Pathways of Behavioral, Economic, and Psychosocial Transformations through Lived Experiences in Rural Uganda
authors: Lukas Neuwirth, Khamisi Musanje, Karen Schelleman-Offermans, Mathias Kayanga, Martin Mabunda Baluku
abstract: This longitudinal mixed-methods study (n=32) investigates the mechanisms through which Unconditional Cash Transfers (UCTs) alleviate extreme poverty in rural Uganda. Drawing on in-depth interviews conducted at three timepoints (baseline, n = 32; one month after, n = 32; one year after, n = 11), alongside economic data and standardized psychological measures, we explored changes in lived experiences, examined individual differences and reconstructed personal trajectories following a combined UCT and behavioral micro-intervention. Findings reveal that, for all participants, UCTs initiated a similar three-stage pathway of change. First, they alleviated material scarcity, leading to a state of basic sufficiency that reduced stress, restored cognitive bandwidth, and fostered future orientation. Second, they served as start-up capital for future-oriented investments and microenterprise development. Finally, as participants engaged in their investments, they initiated an upward spiral of self-reinforcing processes that facilitated poverty graduation. Nonetheless, UCTs demonstrated varying effects. For some, they served as economic relief, while for others, they initiated a cycle of multidimensional transformation. These individual differences were explained by the varying degrees to which participants progressed along this pathway and how strongly underlying processes were activated. Eight psychosocial processes emerged as key drivers of transformation; (1) removing scarcity; (2) goal setting and action planning, (3) experiencing positive emotions; (4) improving self-concepts; (5) developing psychological capital; (6) improving social capital; (7) psychological needs fulfillment and (8) behavioral activation. Our results suggest that UCTs must be understood as interventions that directly engage the psychological, social and behavioral dimensions of poverty. However, future research is needed to replicate and expand our findings.

title: Early climate change coverage in news media: A comparison of East and West Germany from 1950-1978
authors: Viktoria Cologna, Alexander Kaurov, Mike S. Schäfer, Naomi Oreskes
abstract: Press coverage of climate change provides a historical window into how different societies perceived climate change at a given time in a given place. For historically significant emitters such as Germany, reconstructing such news coverage provides important insights into public awareness on the issue. We present the first systematic and comparative analysis of early climate change reporting in East and West Germany between 1950 and 1978. We constructed and validated a corpus of relevant articles through keyword searches, manual screening, and large language model-assisted validation, resulting in a final sample of 122 articles, which we analyzed qualitatively. Our analysis identified four roughly chronological discursive phases: 1) observed glacier melting and the greenhouse effect hypothesis; 2) a perceived end of warming due to decreasing temperatures; 3) growing scientific consensus on human-caused climate change and model uncertainties; 4) increasing attention to the risks of climate change. Human-caused climate change was first mentioned in 1957 and then discussed more extensively in the 1960s and 70s. Despite profound ideological differences, the content and development of the four discursive phases were similar in East and West Germany. However, West German coverage focused more strongly on the impacts on future generations and renewable energy, and gave space to minority skeptical voices, whereas East German coverage focused more strongly on climate modification. This analysis sheds light on the beginnings of climate change reporting in Germany and historically contextualizes awareness of the issue in one of the countries that bears legal and ethical responsibility for addressing climate change.

title: How is Social Status Distributed? A Conjoint Experiment on Social Status Judgements in Great Britain
authors: Jonathan Mellon, Jack Bailey, Geoffrey Evans
abstract: Social status is a core aspect of societal inequalities, yet its determinants and distribution remain understudied. We investigate the factors that shape social status judgments in Great Britain using a conjoint survey experiment with 7,680 respondents making 30,720 status assessments. Drawing on the extant literature, we test economic (occupation, income, wealth, education), cultural (leisure activities and supermarket choice), and ascribed (gender, class background, and ethnicity) factors as determinants of social status. Income has a substantial positive effect on status judgments, as do pro-social occupations (teaching and healthcare). Cultural capital, measured through leisure activities and supermarket preferences, plays a major role in status assessments. We also find that housing wealth, private schooling, higher education, and being White British all increase perceived status. We also contribute to understanding what factors distribute the most status by combining our experimental estimates with data on the prevalence of status predictors in the British population. We find that economic factors, particularly income and wealth distribute the most status. Cultural factors distribute less status, with ascribed characteristics like ethnicity and gender distributing the least status across the whole population, despite sizeable individual-level status penalties for ethnic minorities. Finally, we show that while women, ethnic minorities, and people from working class backgrounds have lower status descriptively in the population, the causes of this lower status differ with ethnic minorities and those from working class backgrounds suffering direct ascribed penalties, whereas women’s lower status derives almost entirely from their worse economic situation (particularly lower income). Our findings support multiple sociological theories of status, demonstrating the importance of occupation, economic resources, cultural capital, and racial hierarchies in status judgments. However, economic factors dominate the distribution of status across society.

title: Embattled Identities: Masculinities and Organizational Behavior in the Iranian Sphere of Influence
authors: Vanessa Zorrilla-Muñoz, Manuel Cuerno, Ines Juaristi
abstract: Most research on masculinities in armed conflict and tension focuses on violence and militarization, overlooking how care (Communion) and dominance interact within masculine identities under chronic insecurity. Using data from the Towards Gender Harmony (TGH) project, this study compares gender self-constructions and care stereotypes between Western liberal democracies and societies under Iranian geopolitical influence or chronic conflict, focusing on the integration versus separation of care and dominance in masculine identities. Gender self-concepts (Communion, Dominance, Agency, Weakness, and Precarious Manhood Beliefs, PMB) were analyzed via t-tests and k-means clustering (k = 4); care stereotypes were examined using Bipolar Class Analysis (BCA) to identify latent cognitive structures (construals) regarding the compatibility of communion and agency traits. The Iran & Conflict group scored higher on Communion, Dominance, Agency, and PMB, and lower on Weakness, and showed a distinctive Provider-Protector cluster profile (high Communion, Dominance, and Agency) absent in the Western sample; PMB behaved as an underlying structural condition rather than a profile-specific trait. Male-only analyses replicated and often intensified these differences, except for Weakness, suggesting that difference was driven by the female subsample. BCA also revealed greater heterogeneity in caregiving stereotypes within the Iran & Conflict group. These results show that caregiving and dominance can integrate into a coherent model of protective, provider masculinity under chronic insecurity, challenging simplistic associations between masculinity and violence and highlighting configurations that legitimize male authority through protection and provision. The study contributes to theorizing masculinities and informs interventions on gender norms in conflict-affected regions.

title: Wealth, inequality and deforestation: a scale-dependent relationship
authors: Elodie Adam, Leland Werden, Melissa Chapman
abstract: Understanding how wealth and economic inequality shape global land-use change is both a long-standing and urgent challenge. While existing empirical evidence largely relies on either national-scale metrics of wealth and inequality or small-scale case studies, few analyses combine global scope with local-scale data. Here we do so, linking local wealth and local inequality to satellite-derived deforestation and its proximate drivers for 27,657 household survey clusters across 52 countries. We find that local wealth, rather than inequality, is the stronger predictor of forest loss, but the direction of this effect is not uniform: depending on the country, a one-standard-deviation increase in local wealth is associated with anywhere from a 19% decrease to a 36% increase in the expected deforestation rate, with no discernible effect in most countries. The share of tree cover loss due to permanent agriculture tends to be higher in wealthier clusters, while the share due to shifting cultivation tends to be higher in areas with lower wealth. We further identify clusters with high wealth, low inequality, and low deforestation, to understand the environmental and socioeconomic drivers of these "triple-win" clusters. Triple-win areas tend to cluster spatially, suggesting that district-level analysis is key to identifying policy levers and institutional structures that can reconcile human development with environmental protection.

title: Social complexity is not correlated with wartime trophy-taking in a cross-cultural sample
abstract: The taking of body parts from enemies during war has been widely recorded across cultures through human history. Qualitative research on trophy-taking suggests it was prevalent among small-scale societies to demonstrate warriors’ military skill and increase status, as well as chiefdoms and early states to display leaders’ monopolization of violence and intimidate external populations. Two sets of analyses were conducted to quantitatively test relationships between trophy-taking practices and social complexity in historical societies. For the first, a dataset was built using ethnographic, historical, and archaeological sources for 110 societies to test whether trophy-taking was more likely at intermediate levels of social complexity. For the second set of analyses, data on headhunting practices were analyzed using a dataset of Austronesian-language speaking societies and the Austronesian language phylogeny. The results for both the global and Austronesian analyses did not support a consistent relationship between trophy-taking practices and social complexity. This work assembles a novel dataset of trophy-taking practices for a global sample of societies, and adds to efforts to study patterns of violence and human social complexity with quantitative methods and comparative historical data.

title: Creationism as a Mediating Construct Between Religiosity, Scientific Epistemology, and Science Attitudes: A Secondary Analysis of the Science Attitudes Dataset
abstract: Since publication of the original analyses in Ideological Mosaic: Examining Political and Religious Factors in Science Attitudes (Deraney & Ault, 2025), a secondary exploratory reanalysis of the original dataset using additional statistical procedures and a revised conceptualization of the Evolutionary Attitudes and Literacy Survey, EALS, (Short & Hawley, 2012). The purpose of this reanalysis was not to replace the original findings, but rather to investigate whether the EALS contained multiple theoretically distinct constructs that were obscured by the original composite score (Deraney & Ault, 2025). Keywords: Science Attitudes, Conservatism, Ideology, Religiosity, Scientific Epistemology, Young- Earth Creation, and Politics.

title: Is there a niche for the NAP in mature climate policy frameworks? An analysis of flood risk management in England and its alignment with adaptation policies
authors: Andrew Russell, Aakash Dipak Patel, Isabel Cotton
abstract: The National Adaptation Programme (NAP) in England is a wide-ranging, statutory, 5-yearly plan that, within the Climate Change Act 2008, has a requirement to develop adaptation objectives to manage climate risks. Since NAP1 in 2013, it has been repeatedly assessed as inadequate by many stakeholders. Here, we investigate how and why it has failed, and assess whether there is a niche for a NAP in a well-developed environmental risk management policy space. We conducted a survey (n=112) that collected quantitative and rich qualitative responses, alongside 4 interviews, with flood risk management (FRM) professionals from England to examine how well the NAP has integrated into this sector, and which policy gaps the NAP could fill. The results indicate that the NAP is much less important to FRM professionals than other relevant strategies and policies, and that its goal or ambition was articulated poorly compared to other policies or plans; the NAP ranked second-bottom for both criteria out of 12 relevant strategies and policies presented. The factors seen as inhibiting adaptation integration were: fragmented governance; avoiding big decisions; and funding alignment with protection rather than resilience measures. Arbitrary targets linked to infrastructure (eg. number of properties better protected) were seen as a barrier to working towards a resilient society. There was significant support for using progress measures more relevant to communities, that cut across policy silos and that apply a wider, resilience-focused interpretation of risk management (eg. saving lives, reforming funding approaches, greater social equity, ensuring insurance availability).

title: Assessing the Trust Crisis in European Security: A New Approach to Measuring Unthinking Trust
abstract: Trust between the United States and its European allies appears to be in crisis, but our knowledge of the exact extent and consequences of this crisis is limited. To address this knowledge gap, we propose a novel approach for measuring deep, unthinking trust in public opinion. We conceptualize unthinking trust as the unquestioned expectation that others will reciprocate cooperation. We qualitatively capture this expectation through open-ended responses in a survey, which we then systematically code, creating a quantitative measure of unthinking trust. We apply our approach to study how recent breaches of trust affect unthinking trust among the German public in two key NATO allies, the UK and the US. Our findings show that a vignette reminding German respondents of Brexit and its aftermath significantly reduces unthinking trust in the UK. A comparable vignette reminding respondents of recent US behavior toward its European allies does not measurably affect unthinking trust in the US, presumably due to salience effects. Furthermore, we find that the Brexit treatment significantly affects respondents’ policy preferences, making them more wary of multilateral security cooperation and, surprisingly, of a national strengthening of defense. A mediation analysis shows that the mechanism of unthinking trust contributes to these effects.

title: Digital Doubles: How does AI-generated imagery affect human engagement with biodiversity conservation?
authors: Maya Mukherjee, Diogo Veríssimo, Amy Hinsley
abstract: 1. Wildlife images created by generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are rapidly growing in quantity and sophistication. Viewing these AI images could influence how people perceive and understand the real natural world, affecting their reactions to real wildlife imagery and potentially in direct wildlife interactions. 2. In this study, we look at how people donate money for conservation purposes to real and AI-generated birds, as well as whether they can accurately discriminate between images in these categories. We further investigate how participant moderating factors and perceived artificiality (i.e. how much an image looks AI-generated) affect these outcomes. 3. Using the contingent valuation method to assess willingness-to-donate, we found that participants award AI-generated and real bird images donation amounts that are not statistically discernible. However, greater perceived artificiality of an image was associated with higher donation amounts. No demographic factors significantly influenced donation behaviour. 4. We also found that participants were able to correctly identify AI vs real images. A nature relatedness score measuring how connected participants were to nature being the only factor to positively predict ability to accurately choose between real and AI images. 5. These findings indicate the potential risk of AI-generated imagery replacing real nature imagery and experience, with artificial representations of wildlife being valued equally to real biodiversity. Conservationists must focus on promoting nature relatedness and real-life, direct nature experiences to combat AI-generated misinformation and decreased understanding of ecological realities.

title: Participatory Narrative Inquiry as an Aligned Approach for Understanding and Addressing Queer Impostor Phenomenon with Bisexual+ Femmes
authors: Devin Madden, Timnit Berhane, Christine Marie “Lovely” Luis Torres Nunez, Alana López, Daniel Eisen, Jean M. Breny, Talina Corvus
abstract: Queer impostor syndrome, as it is colloquially called, is a clear nod to the well-researched concept of impostor phenomenon (IP). Bi+ people experience a disproportionate burden of mental distress and are at the forefront of community dialogues about feelings of queer impostorism, but those discussions are lacking from scientific literature. There is a need for more research with bi+ people for bi+ people, and participatory methods are critical for ensuring responsiveness to this marginalized populations’ needs. This equity-driven study leveraged participatory narrative inquiry to elevate the voices of bisexual+ femmes who self-identify with experiences of queer impostorism as it relates to their sexual identity. Twelve bi+ femmes from New York City shared and analyzed their stories and the stories of their research cohort to characterize QIP for bi+ femmes. This paper details the participatory narrative inquiry process, a community-engaged research approach that asks participants to analyze their own stories and data to yield richer, more resonant results and strategies to bring research-to-action. This manuscript offers researchers insight, through the case study of this research project, into a less traditionally considered qualitative method that allows for meaningful engagement across the research lifespan and may be particularly well-suited for bisexuality research.

title: (No) Longer Dependent: The Association between Reception and Civic Integration Policies and Social Assistance Dependency Among Refugees in the Netherlands
abstract: We analysed how key aspects of refugees’ reception and civic integration experiences relate to their probability of exiting social assistance for employment in the Netherlands. We focused on the duration of stay in reception centres, relocations between centres, completion of the civic integration program, and the language level of the integration diploma. We used administrative data on approximately 95,000 refugees who received refugee residence permits between 2014 and 2022. We conducted robustness analyses using a cohort of approximately 21,000 Syrian refugees who received residence permits between 2014 and 2016 and representative survey data on 2,553 members of this cohort, which allowed us to control for pre-migration education and employment. Multilevel linear probability discrete-time survival models showed distinct gender patterns. Among men, the monthly hazard of exiting social assistance increased until approximately three years after housing and subsequently declined, whereas among women it increased gradually throughout the observation period. Prolonged stays in reception centres were associated with a lower hazard of employment among men, particularly among those who stayed for more than two years, and this disadvantage persisted over time. Among women, the differences by reception duration were small and inconsistent. Relocations had a small and temporary association with employment. Completing civic integration was strongly associated with labour market entry for men and women, and these differences remained substantial after five to six years after housing. B1- and B2-level integration diplomas were generally associated with a higher probability of exiting social assistance than A2-level diplomas.

title: Does Governing Cost Parties Attention on Facebook? Incumbency, Coalitions and Engagement in Europe, 2010 to 2020
abstract: Governing parties tend to lose votes, and junior coalition partners often lose more. Does governing also cost parties attention on social media? I use 660,307 posts from 109 official party pages in 16 European countries, collected through CrowdTangle and covering January 2010 to September 2020, and code each party's place in the national cabinet from ParlGov, with corrections. Fifty-six pages changed status during the period, through 49 entries into government and 43 exits. I compare each party with itself in and out of government, relative to other parties in the same country and month. While in government, a party's posts drew about 18% fewer likes, comments, shares and reactions than the same party's posts in opposition (95% CI 4% to 30%), with the same estimate for the head of government's party and for junior partners. The difference between them lies in volume. The head of government's party posted somewhat more and kept its total engagement, while junior partners posted about 15% less and drew about 25% less in total, an estimate whose interval includes no change. The cost builds with time in office: in its first year the head of government's party drew no less than in opposition, and in its third and fourth years about 40% less. Leaving government did not restore engagement within the two years I can observe. Governing parties' posts were shared less and drew fewer angry reactions. I find no difference between populist and other parties. Event studies around entries and exits are noisy, and parties that entered government had usually gained attention in the year before, so I treat the results as descriptive rather than causal.

title: Inequality of CO₂ Emissions. Carbon Footprint, Socioeconomic Correlates, and Adoption of E-Technology
authors: Andreas Diekmann, Felix Ries, Tom Behringer
abstract: We estimate the carbon footprint of the German resident population from the first wave of the German Longitudinal Environmental Study (GLEN), a large register-based probability sample, using a comprehensive module that measures housing, mobility, diet, and consumption at the individual level. Emissions are strongly right-skewed, averaging 8.6 tons of CO₂ equivalents per capita (9.7 including public infrastructure), and roughly two-thirds of the population emit below the mean. A person at the 90th percentile emits 3 times as much as one at the 10th. The four sectors contribute to total emissions as follows: Mobility 3.6 tons, housing 2.2, diet 1.6, and consumption 1.2. A source decomposition shows that inequality is overwhelmingly driven by mobility. This sector accounts for more than 40 percent of emissions but nearly 80 percent of total footprint inequality. A large part of the amount and variance of mobility is due to flights. Emissions rise with income (elasticity 0.22) and education, while environmental concern and Green Party preference are associated with lower footprints net of sociodemographic characteristics. The adoption of low-carbon technologies, such as heat pumps, solar energy, and electric cars, increases with income and favors homeowners. Finally, we discuss the distributional implications for carbon pricing.

title: Conceptualising EU foreign policy change
abstract: This is chapter 4 from the monograph "Crisis and Change in European Foreign Policy". The book centralizes a set of questions: What happens to European foreign policy arrangements after a crisis hits? Is EU foreign policy changed as a consequence and if so, how and by whom exactly? And crucially: do things actually change? While policy changes on a national level after a sudden crisis have been investigated, little has been done to find out how those processes work exactly within the EU. In this book, Ikani studies the decision-making processes of the European Union, to find out which factors determine if and how the EU decides to change its foreign policy course after crisis. After explaining some of the theory, the book addresses five recent crises, as well as the policy changes that were made as a result: the Arabic uprisings, the Ukraine crisis of 2013/2014, the 'security crisis' that followed, the disinformation crisis, and the 2015 refugee crisis. Based on these cases Ikani created an analytical framework that students and researchers can use when looking to study policy changes in a different context. For example, if they want to know what the impact of the current war in Ukraine might be on European defense policies. But it can also be used to study how a worldwide crisis such as the COVID pandemic will effect domestic and foreign policies.

title: What Does Living in Extreme Poverty Look Like? Exploring Lived Realities in Rural Uganda
authors: Lukas Neuwirth, Khamisi Musanje, Mathias Kayanga, Martin Mabunda Baluku, Karen Schelleman-Offermans
abstract: This qualitative cross-sectional study explored how extreme poverty is experienced in rural Uganda’s Busoga region. Thirty-two semi-structured individual interviews were conducted with adults screened for severe deprivation using the $2.15/day threshold and Multidimensional Poverty Index criteria. Transcripts were analysed via hybrid thematic analysis. Participants reported experiencing pervasive scarcity, unsafe housing, constrained water and sanitation, food insecurity, and limited healthcare. These conditions produced experiences of chronic stress, emotional fatigue, diminished agency, blocked aspirations, irregular livelihoods, and strained relationships alongside fragile community support. Narratives indicated these psychological, behavioural and social patterns were consequences of financial scarcity, suggesting a self-perpetuating poverty cycle.

title: When AI Performs Journalism: Delegation and Journalistic Roles in Collective News Production
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly involved in selecting, interpreting, and generating news content. This conceptual article examines what that involvement means for journalistic role theory and news production. Building on the journalistic role performance framework, we argue that AI can materially shape role performance without possessing a corresponding role conception or perception. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of the architecture of delegation to explain variation in this relationship: the arrangement by which content-shaping operations are assigned to AI, normative orientations are translated into technical instructions, and outputs are incorporated into news. Role performance should align less closely with normative orientations as AI takes on broader, more discretionary, and more consequential functions, and more closely when those orientations guide its use and outputs are substantively reviewed and traceable. These effects are role-specific because their direction and magnitude depend on how each operation affects the practices through which particular roles become manifest. Depending on these conditions, delegation may amplify or displace roles or alter their combination, and may produce performances that were neither intended by journalists nor meaningfully encoded in organizational instructions. We further argue that, as AI-mediated performances become routinized and organizationally rewarded, they may feed back into professional culture and reshape normative orientations.

title: Empirical evidence of negative attitudes to Rroma, Sinti, and Yenish in Switzerland
authors: Didier Ruedin, Anaïd Lindemann, Lisa Stalder
abstract: We provide empirical evidence of negative attitudes to Rroma, Sinti, and Yenish in Switzerland, people who are commonly associated with an itinerant way of life. A large-scale representative survey was implemented in Switzerland in 2019 (N=3,004), including two survey experiments with split samples to vary whether, for the same behaviours, the descriptions refer to an itinerant way of life or not. The survey reveals negative attitudes and limited knowledge of Rroma, Sinti, and Yenish in Switzerland. Negative attitudes to these communities are partially a reflection of a negative evaluation of the perceived impact of an itinerant way of life. Given that most Rroma, Sinti, and Yenish do not actually pursue an itinerant way of life, raising awareness in the majority population may help reduce negative attitudes.

title: Do Populists Win on Facebook? The Engagement Premium of Populist Parties in Europe, 2010 to 2020
abstract: Do populist parties get more attention on Facebook than other parties, and is that true everywhere? I use 669,760 posts from 112 official party pages in 17 European countries, posted between January 2010 and September 2020, with 186,939 posts from 74 party leaders as a second sample. I classify parties as populist, far right or far left using the PopuList, an expert classification, year by year, and add vote shares and government membership from ParlGov. I compare each post with posts by other parties in the same country and month. A typical post by a populist party received about 2.5 times as many likes, comments, shares and reactions as a post by another party of the same size and government status. Populist radical left parties had the largest premium (about 5.4 times), populist radical right parties about 2.3 times and other populists about 1.5 times. I find no premium for far-left parties that are not populist, and no separate premium for Euroscepticism. The premium differs a lot between countries: it was large in Spain, the United Kingdom, Norway, Sweden, Hungary and France, and I cannot detect it in Slovenia, Luxembourg, Slovakia, Finland, Greece or Switzerland. Bigger audiences account for more than half of it. Populist pages had about 1.9 times the page likes of other parties with the same vote share, but at equal page size a premium of about 1.5 times remained. Populist posts drew a higher share of angry reactions (4.4% against 2.7% of interactions). I find no detectable change in the premium after Facebook’s January 2018 News Feed change. Also available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23270349

title: What Does a Satellite Campaign Do? Momentum, the Labour Party and Jeremy Corbyn on Facebook in the 2017 General Election
abstract: Satellite campaigns, organisations that campaign for a party without being part of it, became a visible part of British elections in 2017. The best known was Momentum, formed to support Jeremy Corbyn's leadership of the Labour Party. I ask what Momentum's Facebook page did that Labour's own pages did not. I compare all 153 retrievable posts from Momentum's page in the month before the 2017 general election with 278 posts from the Labour Party page and 144 from Corbyn's page, each hand coded for 154 features. The party page ran a campaign for votes: 85% of its posts asked for a vote, 66% made a pledge and 80% used the party slogan. Momentum asked for a vote in 12% of posts. Instead about half its posts asked people to help on the doorstep, volunteer or sign up to campaign, against 3% to 7% on Labour's pages, and it used humour in a quarter of its posts. Corbyn's page was close to the party page overall, but on all eleven reliably coded features where it differed significantly from the party page, it differed in Momentum's direction: less policy, fewer calls to vote, more news clips and more attacks on the opposition leader. On the Labour side of the 2017 campaign, the leader's page sat between a formal party campaign and a satellite that asked its followers to campaign. Version 2 (2026) replaces the 2021 working paper. It reanalyses all codes with formal tests, corrects for multiple comparisons and reports which codes were reliably measured. Also available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23296711

title: Fear Capital
abstract: This article examines fear as a social, economic and political relation. It argues that fear is a form of capital, a social affect that can be amassed, circulated and redistributed to secure legitimacy, expand coercive power and normalise surveillance. It asks why one of the world's safest societies has come to legislate as though besieged, and answers through a genealogy of the Icelandic state's own pacification projects. Against the myth of Nordic exceptionalism, I argue that Iceland is not an exception to the security state but a least‑likely critical case of securitising practices. Taking my cue from Mark Neocleous' theory of pacification, the article interprets bordering and policing as the continual fabrication of social order against a succession of adversaries: the masterless labourer, the “wayward” woman, the communist and the disgruntled worker and, most recently, racialised persons and non‑European immigrant populations. This succession can be unearthed through the state's information records, from the parish ledger and the alien register to wiretaps and official pronouncements. Across these episodes I identify three modalities of fear capital. Fear is fabricated when moral panics become means of discipline and control, and emulated when foreign threat designations are enacted at home. These two modalities are realised when fear yields budgetary allocations, police powers and electoral gains. The article explains how a society with marginal violent crime has come to govern through the fabrication, emulation and vicarious consumption of fear.

title: AI Swarm Intelligence Must Be Studied as a Sociotechnical Phenomenon
authors: Wenchao Dong, Luiz Felipe Santos Vecchietti, Lukasz Olejnik, Signe Riemer-Sørensen, Jonas R. Kunst, Meeyoung cha, Daniel Thilo Schroeder
abstract: The emergence of coordinated autonomous AI agents is fundamentally altering human belief systems and public discourse at scales and speeds that outpace existing characterization methods. This paper argues that AI swarm intelligence, the coordinated influence of autonomous agents on human populations, represents a phase shift that cannot be understood by simply scaling single-agent analysis. Instead, it must be analyzed as a sociotechnical system where societal impact emerges from the tight coupling of individual agent capabilities, multi-agent coordination, and population dynamics. Because the shift from single- to multi-agent systems corresponds to a psychological transition between single- and multiple-source influence, we propose a unified framework and evaluate these systems across operational, individual, and population-level dynamics. We identify concrete research agendas and call on the community to build the evaluation methods, countermeasures, and governance approaches needed to address the long-term societal impact of these coordinated autonomous AI populations. AI assistance disclosure: Claude (Anthropic) was used solely to polish the language of the manuscript. No other AI assistance was used.

title: Japan measures workplace stress but rarely acts on it: fix the response loop, not the test
abstract: Since 2015, Japanese law has required every workplace with 50 or more employees to screen workers for psychological stress once a year. A decade on, the program's effect on mental health remains unproven. We argue that this is not a failure of measurement but of response. The evidence is consistent: completing the stress survey, receiving individual feedback, or attending a physician interview does not by itself improve distress; the only component linked to better outcomes is improvement of the psychosocial work environment, and that step is carried out after only a small minority of assessments. By average annual hours Japan now sits in the middle of the OECD, yet the incidence of very long working weeks remains high and is masked by that average, and the country's suicide rate is among the highest in the comparison. Across countries these structural indicators track outcomes only weakly, which is reason to distrust ecological arguments and to anchor causal claims in individual-level cohorts. We draw on the logic of infectious-disease surveillance, where the speed of the detection-to-response loop matters more than the precision or frequency of measurement, to reframe what a useful stress-monitoring system should optimize. Raising the frequency of individual screening, or lowering its cost, targets the wrong bottleneck. The lever is a fast, low-cost path from a detected problem to a change in the work environment. This is a framework proposal; its central prediction, that closing the loop raises the rate of environmental action, is testable and should be tested.

title: FUBU-CAPITOL: A Large-Scale Twitter Dataset on the U.S. Capitol Attack and Stop the Steal Discourse (2020–2023)
authors: Michael Kreil, Tristan Stöber, Daniel Thilo Schroeder
